Hi Nate,

thanks for your feedback!
It is really inspiring to see the rig getting to work with hamlib :)

I am not sure, which way to go regarding the need for the new digital modes..

Regarding the Kenwood (i should mention, i havent used DStar at all til now) it would make sense to be able to distinguish between D-Star-Voice and D-Star-Repeater...
But i understand that this approach could result in a lot of new modes introduced in the future.

As an alternative one could add just a generic digital mode, but then it would propably not be possible to choose between them via a frontend application (or the application itself has to add some logic regarding the specific rig) in a comfortable way.

So at the moment i think this should be solved in hamlib, propably by adding the modes in a seperate fashion?!

@bagel99
Thanks for your feedback too!
Your approach looks very promising and cleaner than my quick n dirty implementation and i really like your way of using the VFO channel information, i will test your code with the THD74 to see what we could use in common! :)

73, Sebastian

> Hi Nate,

> It is really inspiring to see the rig getting to work with hamlib :)

Yes, it is.  :-)

> I am not sure, which way to go regarding the need for the new digital modes..
> 
> Regarding the Kenwood (i should mention, i havent used DStar at all
> til now) it would make sense to be able to distinguish between
> D-Star-Voice and D-Star-Repeater...  But i understand that this
> approach could result in a lot of new modes introduced in the future.

Indeed.  At the moment, there are 23 modes defined in rig.h.  There are
no digital voice modes defined at present.  The modes are defined in an
enum which, is limited to 31 entries, as I recall, so there would only
be room for eight more mode entries.  Clearly not enough!

> As an alternative one could add just a generic digital mode, but then
> it would propably not be possible to choose between them via a
> frontend application (or the application itself has to add some logic
> regarding the specific rig) in a comfortable way.

As I see it, future radios will probably support the setting of DV modes
in a manner similar to analog radios setting AM, LSB, USB, etc.

> So at the moment i think this should be solved in hamlib, propably by
> adding the modes in a seperate fashion?!

Should this be done through a new set of functions such as
rig_[set|get]_dvmode() and then a new data structure devoted solely to
digital voice modes?

I am going to CC the mailing list, so hopefully we'll get some other
feedback there.

> @bagel99
> Thanks for your feedback too!
> Your approach looks very promising and cleaner than my quick n dirty
> implementation and i really like your way of using the VFO channel
> information, i will test your code with the THD74 to see what we could
> use in common! :)

I hope both of you can collaborate on this!

73, Nate

--------------------8<------------------

#include <stdio.h>

enum small_enum {
    a
};

enum large_enum {
    b = 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF // 2^63-1
};

int main()
{

#ifdef __LP64__
    printf("LP64: %ld %ld %d %lx\n",
           sizeof(enum small_enum),
           sizeof(enum large_enum),
           a,
           b);
#else
    printf("%d %d %d %llx\n",
           sizeof(enum small_enum),
           sizeof(enum large_enum),
           a,
           b);
#endif

    return 0;
}

-------------------->8------------------


I added a bit of text so I could tell the difference.  On Slackware64
14.2 I get:

$ ./lp64
LP64: 4 8 0 7fffffffffffffff

and in the Slackware 14.2 (32 bit VM) I get:

$ ./lp64 
4 8 0 7fffffffffffffff
 
Since the modes are defined as bitmask values and are ORed together in
the rig_caps structure, as I see it, using 64 bit enums only doubles our
present mode space to 63.  As changing this is an ABI/API change, I
think we should future proof this as much as possible.  IMO, the maximum
number of modes should be at a minimum 1024 or unlimited.  SDRs will
likely support all the variations of digi data/voice modes as individual
"modes", so this needs to be a large namespace.

Likewise, the number of "VFOs" and antenna ports need to be
large/unlimited.  How imaginative will split frequency operations
become?

Time to dust off the crystal balls and throw some ideas around.

73, Nate

The default value for the rig_open member of rig_caps is NULL, which nearly all current Icom rigs are set to. In these cases, icom_rig_open is not called and the value of serial_full_duplex in the icom_priv_caps struct is used and not altered. Only if rig_open=icom_rig_open does the test and possible override of serial_full_duplex occur. I did it this way to enure full backward compatibility.

The Yaesu FT-736r has no means to read the radio's settings.  (Though
you can read a value relating to the S meter level, and find out if the
FM Squelch is open/closed.)   ALL other commands are one way, you send,
and have to trust that it happened!

(If the over-the-air messaging system is installed, that can return
received messages to you, but I've never even seen one of those add-on
accessories.)


Some of the Skanti radios too, depending on protocol may, or may not
confirm that a command has "taken", some also use a very slow 2400bd
link, and a byte by byte ACK/NAK type of protocol.  (And then
internally, a 300bd link between the control panel, and the "guts" of
the radio, so can take a second or two, before you can get a
confirmation that what you wanted to happen, has, or not happened.)


However, both those examples are not exactly "mainstream" rigs these
days, but do have niche uses, and fan-bases.

The way the 9700 operates though is you have two completely independent VFOs.The top display has VFOA/B and it's own Main/Sub.The bottom display also has it's own VFOA/B and it's own Main/Sub.So you can, for example, have both on VFOA, or both on VFOB.You should be able to operate WSJT-X completely off of either one in split mode and no VFO swapping going on.
The 0x07 0xd2 cmd allows reading/setting of the Selected/Unselected VFO so, given we know the setup to start with, we can determine VFOA/B.
Users can, of course, mess this all up with twiddling the knobs, that's the biggest downside to this idea that I can think of but I think we already have that problem with Icoms, don't we? I'm of the opinion, at the moment, that eliminating the VFO swap that goes on would be a good thing.  But I could be convinced otherwise.

I'm in the process of fixing implementation of many Icom CI-V commands that currently either do not work at all or work incorrectly when compared to the Hamlib API spec.

However, there's one particular command that is difficult to implement with Icom radios and that is the manual notch frequency (RIG_LEVEL_NOTCHF). Based on Icom radio manuals I've read (and I've checked most of the modern ones >= IC-7000), the scale for adjusting manual notch frequency is simply 0 to 255 without any indication of the actual frequency.

After all, the Hamlib API specifies RIG_LEVEL_NOTCHF as:
    RIG_LEVEL_NOTCHF =      (1 << 15),      /*!< \c NOTCHF -- Notch Freq., arg int (Hz) */

indicating that the argument should be the frequency in Hz.

I'm wondering if anyone knows better whether the notch frequency value for Icom rigs actually corresponds to a specific frequency or if it is relative to, for example, the filter width currently selected?

Thanks for the comments.

@mdblack98 My point is exactly that now it's very difficult to develop a GUI (which I've done) that works properly with Icom rigs. Let me explain:

1) For rigs that conform to Hamlib API (e.g. some Kenwood ones), the value for manual notch is in Hz (as specified in the API docs): the UI can display the unit (Hz) and the value is easy to adjust, e.g. 1500 Hz when using SSB with filter of 2.4kHz.

2) For Icom rigs, the value range is always 0 to 255, which is not in Hz and it is not even a constant scale, as it depends on rig settings. Even if the range (`level_gran`) would be specified by the rig (which it is not currently), the resulting value between 0 and 255 is confusing. Because of the limitations of Icom rigs, the backend does not (and cannot) know the actual value in Hz.

Alternatively, we could add another type of (standardized) manual notch level that is a float value from 0 to 1.0, which does not specify any particular scale or unit, so that a GUI can present the scale and the value in a user-friendly way.

@N0NB @mdblack98 Explaining the problem further: the issue is simply the fact that because of the Hamlib API definition, the UI _must_ assume that the manual notch value unit is Hz and that it is an integer value. It would be more natural to have a floating point value without any unit for Icom rigs. Having the UI display "technical" values where the user just "has to know" what the values mean (and the UI is misleading the user) is something I would like to fix here.

As we are still on the way to Hamlib 4.x release, this would be a good time to add more levels, although it does require new clients to use the new level instead of the old one for Icom rigs. But that's what major releases are useful -- it allows one to break the API (even if this change is not really breaking the API, but simply changing the level definitions, which should be possible with *any* release...)

The manual for the GS-232B says:

> Commands are not echoed by the Control Interface, but a carriage return character 0xD is returned after every command, and also a line feed character 0xA if the command invoked returned data.

This is consistent with what I see, where linux correctly interprets the linefeeds when something is actually returned. This is the crux of the problem: even a single carriage return character would satisfy the read in the gs232b_transaction() function.
I have tried changing the serial port settings, including going to raw mode, and nothing seems to make any difference.  Unfortunately I don't have another computer with a native RS232 interface, so it is not possible for me to check if the GS-232B is actually generating an output or not. Very frustrating.

Thanks again,
Randall.

Hi again,

I have just confirmed with a handheld DSO that the GS-232B does NOT emit any signal at all after being sent a pointing command (e.g. "W180 100").

Example of DSO screen, when the trigger is set to capture a snapshot. (Trigger is on the yellow signal, which is the output of the GS-232B, the cyan signal is the input to the GS232B). In this case, I have just pressed the enter key in a serial console, and the GS-232B returns ">$CRLF" where CR is the carriage return character and LF is the line feed character. This matches what is described in the manual.

![IMG_006](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6964778/62421522-9b38f000-b6d5-11e9-8b4a-55d268610ecb.png)

If I issue a command to get the current pointing ("C"), I see:
![IMG_007](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6964778/62421524-abe96600-b6d5-11e9-8912-dfc4a4be1669.png)

We can't see the command in this instance - the DSO is triggered on the reply from the DS-232B. This indicates there is a delay > 5 ms between receiving the command and responding, which seems reasonable in this case.

When I issue a command to point "W180 100", there is NO response at all from the GS-232B. I have to press enter another time to get the default "$>" response, at which point the DSO will trigger and capture the waveform.

So at this point I can pretty definitively say that the GS-232B is not working as per the manual. Can any other GS-232B users confirm they have seen this behaviour?

Thanks,
Randall VK6WR.

11:04:22  COM6        Status AZ:169.0, EL:0.0

```
You can see that HRD does not look for replies on "write only" commands, only for "query" type commands.

The solution for hamlib is to stop the function gs232b_transaction() in gs232b.c from expecting a reply for "write only" commands. The easiest way to achieve this is to return success after issuing the command successfully if the return buffer is NULL. Here's my one-line diff:

```
rwayth@mypi:~/Hamlib $ git diff gs232a/gs232b.c
diff --git a/gs232a/gs232b.c b/gs232a/gs232b.c
index f2dbbe91..a39537d6 100644
--- a/gs232a/gs232b.c
+++ b/gs232a/gs232b.c
@@ -81,7 +81,8 @@ transaction_write:
 
     /* Always read the reply to know whether the cmd went OK */
     if (!data)
-        data = replybuf;
+        return RIG_OK;
+       //        data = replybuf;
     if (!data_len)
         data_len = BUFSZ;
```

Incidentally, this also fixes the direct "move" commands in rotctl which I just confirmed also did not work (for the same reason) but work after the fix.

Regards,
Randall.

You need to add the -Z switch to see timing info.
write_delay=150 puts a 150ms delay on every character being written which seems a bit excessive although I guess we're not in much of a hurry here.
It sounds like it may be overrunning the serial buffer
You can adjust the write_delay from the command line and see what value works.
rotctl --set-conf=write_delay=50

Not sure of your setup but there are two ways to get debug info.
#1 If you can set up the software to use rigctld is best because then you see what the software is asking for.#2 Using rigctl directly which doesn't require the application.
Let's start with rigctl -- this should work....TS-590S I assume and not TS-590SG?  If SG use -m 237 instead

rigctl -m 231 -r /dev/xxxx -s 9600 -vvvvvAdjust COM port and baud rate to match your setup.
Using the following command this is what I'd expect to see.
V VFOAF 14074000fFrequency: 14074000V VFOBF 14075000fFrequency: 14075000T 1fFrequency: 14075000V VFOAfFrequency: 14074000T 0
You can also run rigctl (and rigctld) requiring the vfo be provided and again you'll get whatever VFO you ask for.rigctl -m 231 -r /dev/xxxx -s 9600 -vvvvv
F VFOA 14074000F VFOB 14075000
f VFOAFrequency: 14074000f VFOB
Frequency: 14075000

In other words it depends on which VFO you ask for as to what frequency you get.Some other software may assume you want the TX VFO when asking for generic frequency...hamlib does not make that assumption.  You get what you ask for regardless of PTT status
Mike

icom_set_mode_with_data calls icom_set_mode, passing the filter width through, and then does a data mode (1A 06, except on IC-7200) call to set data mode to 0 or 1 depending on whether the mode was a PKT one.

The problem is that (at least on the 7300 and 7610, and probably on most newer rigs), the filter width passed to the "set mode" command only affects the non-data filter width, and to change the data filter width, one must pass a filter width to the 1A 06 command. Since hamlib omits this parameter, the width is never changed for packet modes.

It seems easy enough to drag a call to rig2icom_mode/r2i_mode into icom_set_mode_with_data to get the proper width and then pass it along to the datamode command, but perhaps a refactor is in order — should there be one function which outputs icmode/icmode_ext/datamode/datamode_ext and the whole sequence keyed off of those?

Also, to research: are there rigs that support 1A 06, but where it doesn't have a second byte for filter width?

    On Wednesday, November 20, 2019, 02:30:35 PM CST, Andrew Rodland <notifications@github.com> wrote:  
 
 
icom_set_mode_with_data calls icom_set_mode, passing the filter width through, and then does a data mode (1A 06, except on IC-7200) call to set data mode to 0 or 1 depending on whether the mode was a PKT one.

The problem is that (at least on the 7300 and 7610, and probably on most newer rigs), the filter width passed to the "set mode" command only affects the non-data filter width, and to change the data filter width, one must pass a filter width to the 1A 06 command. Since hamlib omits this parameter, the width is never changed for packet modes.

It seems easy enough to drag a call to rig2icom_mode/r2i_mode into icom_set_mode_with_data to get the proper width and then pass it along to the datamode command, but perhaps a refactor is in order — should there be one function which outputs icmode/icmode_ext/datamode/datamode_ext and the whole sequence keyed off of those?

Also, to research: are there rigs that support 1A 06, but where it doesn't have a second byte for filter width?

I think the issue with why I'm seeing the linker fail on MinGW is that in src/sleep.c the sleep() and usleep() functions are wrapped by `#ifdef HAVE_NANOSLEEP` and that macro is not defined in `config.h` as Windows doesn't have nanosleep nor the other two functions.  As a result none of the three functions defined in src/sleep.c show up in the symbol table of src/.libs/sleep.o.

My guess is that for Windows the function in the removed include/hl_sleep.h file or similar will need to be restored.  It sucks, but that's Windows for ya!
In other words, Windows will need a custom nanosleep function provided and only compiled for Windows.

nanosleep should be defined in pthread.h
I'm hoping that including pthread.h in rig.h allows configure to pick up HAVE_NANOSLEEP on Win32

Icom SDR rigs (7300, 7610, 9700, etc.) support sending waterfall data over USB for display on a PC. When the scope data output (command 27 subcommand 20) is enabled, the rig sends a constant stream of unsolicited scope data reports (command 27 subcommand 00), with raw binary payloads, between command responses. Their RS-BA1 remote control software and a few other third-party Windows programs support decoding and displaying it.

I want to make something similar but cross-platform, and of course I don't want my program to take sole ownership of the serial port; I want to have rigctld running and do other hamlib things at the same time. Practically speaking, this means that hamlib needs to be the one handling the scope data.

I don't care if hamlib interprets it, but what I would hope for would be
   
   - For hamlib not to desync or show any behavior difference to uninterested clients, when connected to a rig with scope data output enabled.
   - For a TCP client to have a way to subscribe to the scope data, receiving it as it comes in, with sensible framing (It could also be used for other kinds of transcieve data, e.g. Icoms will tell you about frequency changes and PTT toggles if you ask... but I don't care if it doesn't). I wouldn't mind if starting one of these subscriptions made the socket totally unable to issue other commands (to avoid framing problems).

I think this should be more or less possible with the existing event loop code in hamlib, and I'm willing to make an attempt at it myself, but I wanted to run the approach by someone first, and get some input, to increase the chances of actually getting a patch accepted.

icom_set_mode_with_data calls icom_set_mode, passing the filter width through, and then does a data mode (1A 06, except on IC-7200) call to set data mode to 0 or 1 depending on whether the mode was a PKT one.

The problem is that (at least on the 7300 and 7610, and probably on most newer rigs), the filter width passed to the "set mode" command only affects the non-data filter width, and to change the data filter width, one must pass a filter width to the 1A 06 command. Since hamlib omits this parameter, the width is never changed for packet modes.

It seems easy enough to drag a call to rig2icom_mode/r2i_mode into icom_set_mode_with_data to get the proper width and then pass it along to the datamode command, but perhaps a refactor is in order — should there be one function which outputs icmode/icmode_ext/datamode/datamode_ext and the whole sequence keyed off of those?

Also, to research: are there rigs that support 1A 06, but where it doesn't have a second byte for filter width?

Based on my understanding (and by reading the IC-7300 or IC-7610 manuals), the "Scope waveform data" (what the manual calls it) consists of bytes, which resemble FFT results.

On page 19-12 of the IC-7300 FULL MANUAL:

    The transceiver outputs the drawn waveform data.
    The data range or data length of the waveform
    data is judged by the controller. (The data range is
    basically the same as the display size of the scope
    on the controller.)

    Data range: 0~160
    Data length: 475

I think the above means that the packet contains 475 bytes with values from a minimum of 0 to maximum of 160 for each frequency "bucket" (as in FFT). The "Scope waveform data" includes some header bytes, which indicate the edges or the center of the waterfall frequencies, so one can calculate which frequency each "bucket" indicates.

It seems that the data length and range are different for IC-7610 (and I'd assume they may be different for IC-9700 too), but otherwise the format seems to be similar.

It would certainly be nice to be able to extract this data in Hamlib, but the issue is that it is very Icom-specific. It's not I/Q, audio or even bitmap data, but some kind of pseudo-FFT results, which allow you to plot waterfall based on the intensity levels for the frequency buckets.

EDIT: It's also worth keeping in mind that the data rate for the waterfall data is quite low: the maximum output speed is 115 200 bps even with the USB connection, as it shares the CI-V control interface. This means that the update rate may not be particularly smooth...

It's *basically* a bitmap ­— @mikaelnousiainen  has the details about right. It's a bunch of bytes, each one represents the energy in a frequency bin, 0 is least, more is more, details are dependent on the rig and on the various scope settings. The complexity of interpreting it is why I wasn't gunning for hamlib to interpret these messages — I was just looking for a way to pass them through to a client that can.

Would it make sense to do the following to extract the data to clients:

1) Implement some (or why not all) of the 27 xx CI-V commands as Icom-specific (but not model-specific) ext params (not ext levels, as the feature isn't directly RX or TX related), so that Hamlib clients can turn on/off and configure the waterfall. The commands seem to be identical (with some additions in 7610) for IC-7300, IC-7610 and IC-9700 at least. There may be other rigs that support this too, but I haven't checked. This way one could just enable the spectrum support on rigs that have it.

2) Design a push-based response format for rig-specific data. There should be an indicator in the beginning of this response about the contents, e.g. `Data: ICOM_WATERFALL` or similar. In my opinion, Hamlib should do some interpretation of the waterfall data and expose it in a format that is easier to parse by the clients. The Hamlib protocol is text-based after all, so we can't (and shouldn't) even push the binary data directly out. A simple way (key-value pairs, e.g. `Center: 3700000 Hz`, like with other command responses) to express the waterfall edges/dimensions with Base64-encoded or even numeric hex data for the waterfall bytes could be enough. Another option would be to use a JSON object to contain all of the fields and waterfall data. That would make parsing relatively easy in most clients and the boundaries of the response would be easy to interpret.

This would not be a "generic" solution for all rigs, but rather just a way to pass the Icom-specific data to clients that wish to receive it. It would not break existing implementations, as the client would have to turn on reception of the waterfall data. However, we would probably need one more setting somewhere for the clients to indicate that they support push data, so that Hamlib could send the push data for *all* clients interested (and not break ones that do not support it). After all, Hamlib needs to support multiple clients where some of them may not be able to handle the push data. So this would be an opt-in extension of the Hamlib protocol.

With the data format Icom provides, I'm not sure we can do anything that is more generic. I suspect other rigs may expose similar functionality in the future too -- do you know if the latest SDR-based Kenwood, Yaesu or possibly the upcoming Elecraft K4 support exposing waterfall/audio/IQ data? I've got the impression that K4 would offer some of this at least.

Yes, sorry. I tested the built-in GPIO support and it works now.

Our fork works fine, however as it turns out, this feature was already in Hamlib, but not documented in the manpage!

Basically, what you want to do is figure out the physical GPIO pin number of the wanted PTT pin. You can do it by data-mining datasheets, or you can install wiringPi and use the `gpio readall` command which will print a graphic representation of the pin header on your Pi (you'll need the 'BCM' columns from it). Let's say you want pin 17. Then you can use the PTT like this:
```
sudo rigctld -P GPIO -p 17
```
Then connect to `rigctld` with whichever program supports it (QSSTV does, I didn't test WSJT-X).

After extensive testing between me and Mike, we've narrowed down this issue to a quirk of Chinese USB-to-UART cables.  For anyone reading this, please check whether there is continuity between the TX and RX pads on the board.

If there is, there will be either a solder blob or a zero-ohm jumper (which looks like a resistor, but with a "0" on the package) on the reverse side of the board that bridges the pads.  Remove this bridge and the TX and RX lines will be separated.

Please note that if this issue exists, you will need to check that the cable itself has all of the wires you need to run to the radio.  In my case, the cable only had two wires, and I had to replace it with another 6-pin DIN cable.  Please reference page 11 or page 44 for the pinout for this cable.

I submitted a patch to fix that and put some notes about the needed versions of swig and lua.

Our fork works fine, however as it turns out, this feature was already in Hamlib, but not documented in the manpage!

Basically, what you want to do is figure out the physical GPIO pin number of the wanted PTT pin. You can do it by data-mining datasheets, or you can install wiringPi and use the gpio readall command which will print a graphic representation of the pin header on your Pi (you'll need the 'BCM' columns from it). Let's say you want pin 17. Then you can use the PTT like this:
sudo rigctld -P GPIO -p 17

Then connect to rigctld with whichever program supports it (QSSTV does, I didn't test WSJT-X).

Is this function generic enough to warrant its own API function? If it is only an Icom specific operation, then the API should not be so burdened. There is a mechanism to access all those extended operations that Icom offer. I recently generalized this in my recent merge so that these functions do not need specific code, but simply an additional line in two look-up tables.

There is an argument for adding g/set_ext_func() to the API as there are many operations that are not a semantic match for the g/set_ext_parm() functions. These are operations that switch things on & off (the voice keyer being one such), rather than a device setting that the *parm operations are intended for.

I could add & implement the g/set_ext_func() API function & add the voice keyer operation to my Icom extended operation infrastructure. This would then invoked from rigctl by: "U voicekey n" or called from code via the API by: "set_ext_func(rig, TOK_VOICEKEY, n)"

The antenna command had to be "broken" as it was did not work for current (and future rigs)....Icom rigs in particular.
4.0 has not been officially released yet and is still under development.
This is the first thing we've had to do that breaks the ABI.
The intent right now is this...which, as I said, is still under development and subject to change.
Y Antenna OptionAntenna will be 1-based.  The Option flag right now only applies to some Icom rigs where you can set an antenna to Rx-only.  I can easily imagine this will expand in the future.
y AntennaAntenna will be 1-based.  Antenna#0 will return the currently select antenna and it's option setting which you can ignore (defaults to 0 if rig doesn't have any Option capability)
If you're interfacing to rigctld you can send a "y" command by itself and if you get prompted with Antenna: then it's the new version.
I'll update the man page.

Thanks for asking.

I'm developing (or have developed for the past 2 years, actually) a piece of software called Web Radio Control. It's a web-based remote control application that is based on Hamlib and Janus WebRTC gateway (to take care of audio I/O). The core idea is that you will need only a web browser and a Raspberry Pi (or a similar Linux-based computer) to control your rig. The software is using Hamlib capabilities extensively to expose all possible functionality of the radios/rotators in the UI. More recently, there have been some alternatives (such as RigPi) that offer similar functionality, but it wasn't the case when I started the project.

Web Radio Control has been tested actively by ~20-30 Finnish radio amateurs, so I've been able to collect some feedback and do testing with different sets of hardware. I'm about to create a proper website for the project during this spring (currently, we have only a site that documents the installation procedure and it's still Finnish-only). The software is not open source (and probably will not be, as being a "community manager/maintainer" for a hobby project of mine isn't something I wish to do). However, I'm happy to contribute to open-source projects that I use -- like I have done with Hamlib. My main goal with Hamlib has been so far to improve capabilities and add functions/levels/parameters to enhance remote control possibilities.

Here are some screenshots, if you're interested (again, the website is unfortunately in Finnish only, but will be translated later):

https://doc.webradiocontrol.tech/getting-started/screenshots/

There's also a mailing list (though the international side of it is still inactive, as we have a separate subgroup for Finnish users): https://wrc-users.groups.io/g/main -- I'll be making announcements there once the website and proper systems for licensing/download are set up.

What baud rate are you running at?
There are 3 parameters you can try adding to the the rigctl command line....preferably in this order
timeoutwrite_delay
post_write_delay

timeout defaults to 200ms -- so try increasing it by 50ms increments up to 500ms to see if that works.--set-conf=timeout=250
write_delay is a delay after each byte written and defaults to 0.  Increase in 10ms increments up to 50ms.  Anything more than that would seem to be overly excessive.--set-conf=write_delay=10
post_write_delay is a delay after writing a command which isn't really any different in this case from timeout.  It also defaults to 0 so could be incremented by 50ms too.

As Mike stated, working from a Git tree can be troublesome as sometimes
you need to use 'git clean -dxf' to remove any and all generated files
in the working tree and completely delete everything under the build
directory (if you're using a VPATH) build.

The simplest method is to use the daily snapshots as they're already
set up so that libtool or any of the other GNU Autotools are not
required to be installed on your system.  However, if you're testing
from Mike's tree this won't help.  Better then just to do a clean 'git
clone' and working from there.

My apologies, I should probably clarify further as to what's going on.

The PR linked in OP is for a proposed GUI element in FreeDV that displays the radio's current mode and turns red if it's not what's expected for the radio's current band (LSB <= 40m, USB >= 20m). The basic functionality of this works on all tested platforms (Mac, Linux and Windows 10) in that when the Start button's pressed, the current code in the PR is able to make the needed rig_* calls to retrieve the current frequency and mode (src/hamlib.cpp [lines 192-214](https://github.com/drowe67/freedv-gui/pull/47/files#diff-192b42b90f0378588953e0aa18ddf023R192)).

A nice to have feature, however, is the ability for FreeDV to track changes to frequency and mode and update the aforementioned GUI element as that occurs. Based on what I've been able to find in the Hamlib documentation thus far, this seems to be accomplished through the use of code similar to the following:

`rig_set_freq_callback(m_rig, &hamlib_freq_cb, this);`
`rig_set_mode_callback(m_rig, &hamlib_mode_cb, this);`
`rig_set_trn(m_rig, RIG_TRN_POLL);`

followed by specific implementations of the registered callback functions to do whatever desired actions the developer wants.

In my testing with the above code, the callbacks seem to properly be getting executed within a second or so after changing band and mode on the tested radio itself (Elecraft KX3)--but only on Mac (macOS Catalina) and Linux (Ubuntu 18.04 LTS). When the same code is run on Windows 10, only the initial state update mentioned above seems to occur and not the expected state tracking.

Anyway, the reason why I concluded that sigaction() seems to be necessary for rig_set_trn() is that rig_set_trn() calls add_trn_poll_rig(), which is wrapped such that the implementation becomes simply a stub that returns -RIG_ENIMPL if HAVE_SIGACTION isn't defined. In addition, there's a second #ifdef wrapper in rig_set_trn() [that doesn't even bother calling add_trn_poll_rig()](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/7c7ecef678c62eaed10bacab548f99f64ce65811/src/event.c#L763) if HAVE_SETITIMER isn't defined. 

All that said, as the PR is now, the basic feature works as intended. It just would be nice to be able to do the above on Windows as well, even if it means Hamlib has to have Windows-specific code to simulate what it's doing on other platforms. Maybe this should be tagged to indicate that it's a feature request rather than an actual issue?

BTW, @N0NB, good call on not being able to read frequency/mode on some rigs. I'll have to see how to handle that on the FreeDV side (maybe by not enabling that control for them?)

Why don't you ask directly for freq & mode during your own polling cycle rather than relying on the rig to send it to you async?

As far as I know more rigs will answer rig_get_freq and rig_get_mode than will give async changes.

de Mike W9MDB

Actually, speaking of rig support, I did try calling rig_set_trn() with RIG_TRN_RIG instead of RIG_TRN_POLL and found that it didn't work with the radio I was using it with (in retrospect, probably due to lack of support as you mention). However, RIG_TRN_POLL did work with the radio I was using. 

In fact, it appears that Hamlib only does capability checking if using RIG_TRN_RIG (see [here](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/master/src/event.c#L746)). Using polling seems to result in [search_rig_and_poll() getting called](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/master/src/event.c#L368) regardless of radio support; handling for rigs that don't support e.g. frequency queries happens in there.

Anyway, it looks like there is some sort of handling in Hamlib already that could be tapped into for any Windows specific implementation if the library itself is extended in the future. Alternatively, it could just be used as a basis for an implementation on the FreeDV side.

I've never really looked at that before but I believe the meaning is intended to be this:
RIG_TRN_OFF -- can't get any info from rig at allRIG_TRN_POLL -- get info by polling the rig(s)RIG_TRN_RIG -- rig(s) can provide async data
This hasn't been documented very well so needs to be improved.A lot of this is based on Icom's CI-V protocol which is different than everybody else's as you can have multiple rigs on the bus.

actually quite simple using these terminal commands:

	sudo apt update
	sudo apt upgrade

These two will ensure your system is up-to-date for security fixes and
other bug fixes in various packages.  The first time you do this the
list will likely be quite large and take some time.  When done more
frequently, the updates may only involve one or a handful of packages.

To install a given package, in this case libtool-bin:

	sudo apt install libtool-bin

However, you don't need that package installed to bootstrap hamlib.  I
need to correct the README.developer file on that package.

To find a specific package:

	apt search "midnight commander"

will return a list of packages with those words including the "mc"
package which is the Swiss Army Chainsaw of file managers.  I've been
using it since first starting with Slackware Linux in the autumn of
1996.

Another packager manager I have used for at least 20 years is "aptitude".
It may not be installed by default and it is actually fairly slow but it
has a TUI that is reasonably easy to navigate.

rotator = Rotator(settings.ROT_MODEL, settings.ROT_BAUD, settings.ROT_PORT)

Also it may be an easy fix.  Sounds like the Minion is timing out.
The default inter-char delay for the TS440 is 20ms.
write_delay: "Delay in ms between each byte sent out" Default: 0, Value: 20 Range: 0.0..1000.0, step 1.0


So try changing it to 0
 rigctl -m 202 -r /dev/ttyACM0 -vvvvv --set-conf=write_delay=0

> 
> ```

> 11:04:16  COM6        Purging channel 000003BC, flags 0000000F
> 11:04:16  COM6        Set position> Send 57-32-38-38-20-30-30-30-0D
> 11:04:18  COM6        Setting position to AZ:288.0° (288.7°, Curr: 143.0°), EL:0.0° (0.0°, Curr: 1.0°), North: Yes
> 11:04:18  COM6        Purging channel 000003BC, flags 0000000F
> 11:04:18  COM6        Set position> Send 57-32-38-38-20-30-30-30-0D
> 11:04:19  COM6        Get status> Send 43-32-0D
> 11:04:19  COM6        Get status> Recv 41-5A-3D-31-35-34-20-20-45-4C-3D-30-30-30-0D-0A-00-00-00-00
> 11:04:19  COM6        Status AZ:154.0, EL:0.0
> 11:04:20  COM6        Setting position to AZ:288.0° (288.5°, Curr: 154.0°), EL:0.0° (0.0°, Curr: 0.0°), North: Yes
> 11:04:20  COM6        Purging channel 000003BC, flags 0000000F
> 11:04:20  COM6        Set position> Send 57-32-38-38-20-30-30-30-0D
> 11:04:22  COM6        Get status> Send 43-32-0D
> 11:04:22  COM6        Get status> Recv 41-5A-3D-31-36-39-20-20-45-4C-3D-30-30-30-0D-0A-00-00-00-00
> 11:04:22  COM6        Status AZ:169.0, EL:0.0
> ```
> 
> You can see that HRD does not look for replies on "write only" commands, only for "query" type commands.
> 
> The solution for hamlib is to stop the function gs232b_transaction() in gs232b.c from expecting a reply for "write only" commands. The easiest way to achieve this is to return success after issuing the command successfully if the return buffer is NULL. Here's my one-line diff:
> 
> ```
> rwayth@mypi:~/Hamlib $ git diff gs232a/gs232b.c
> diff --git a/gs232a/gs232b.c b/gs232a/gs232b.c
> index f2dbbe91..a39537d6 100644
> --- a/gs232a/gs232b.c
> +++ b/gs232a/gs232b.c
> @@ -81,7 +81,8 @@ transaction_write:
>  
>      /* Always read the reply to know whether the cmd went OK */
>      if (!data)
> -        data = replybuf;
> +        return RIG_OK;
> +       //        data = replybuf;
>      if (!data_len)
>          data_len = BUFSZ;
> ```
> 
> Incidentally, this also fixes the direct "move" commands in rotctl which I just confirmed also did not work (for the same reason) but work after the fix.
> 
> Regards,
> Randall.

Yes, for the python extension it's not necessary to link with libpython for python-3.8 or newer, upstream PR: https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/12946

Python 3.8 release notes:
https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.8.html

```
On Unix, C extensions are no longer linked to libpython except on Android and Cygwin. It is now
possible for a statically linked Python to load a C extension built using a shared library Python.
(Contributed by Victor Stinner in bpo-21536.)
```

I think you should use pkgconfig.

I.e. pkgconfig for python-3.7:
```
$ cat /usr/lib64/pkgconfig/python3.pc
# See: man pkg-config
prefix=/usr
exec_prefix=/usr
libdir=/usr/lib64
includedir=/usr/include

Name: Python
Description: Python library
Requires: 
Version: 3.7
Libs.private: -lcrypt -lpthread -ldl  -lutil
Libs: -L${libdir} -lpython3.7m
Cflags: -I${includedir}/python3.7m
```
And pkgconfig for python-3.8:
```
$ cat /usr/lib64/pkgconfig/python3.pc
# See: man pkg-config
prefix=/usr
exec_prefix=/usr
libdir=/usr/lib64
includedir=/usr/include

Name: Python
Description: Build a C extension for Python
Requires:
Version: 3.8
Libs.private: -lcrypt -lpthread -ldl  -lutil -lm
Libs:
Cflags: -I${includedir}/python3.8
```
Notice there is no -lpython, i.e.:
```
$ pkg-config --libs python3 #python-3.7
-lpython3.7m 
$ pkg-config --libs python3 #python-3.8
```

The connection looks fine, and I can confirm the mount receives command, per Issue 2 below.
c:\Program Files (x86)\hamlib-w32-3.3\bin>rotctl -m 1801 -r COM3 -vvvv

This appears to be the same issue as previously reported here:

Issue 2: set_pos fails if elevation argument greater than 1.50 deg (regardless of az which works fine for elevation values <=1.5). Here's a successful slew to 1.5 deg and failure at 1.51:

set_pos: error = Invalid parameter

This seems suspiciously close to 1.57 rad, which is 90 deg elevation, which one might expect to get rejected.  I wonder if there might be a missing deg->rad conversion?

Logs available if needed, but the above snippets capture the parts of interest.

What John's solution is after is to allow "input boxes" such as "localhost:19090" . The current hamlib "serial to TCP" fallback mechanism cannot cope with that.

So in the current situation if put into the input box (that is, the string in rigport.pathname)

/dev/ttyUSB0                ==> hamlib will try to open serial port  (fine)
:19090                          ==> hamlib will try to open TCP (fine)
192.168.1.50:19090      ==> hamlib will try to open TCP (fine)
localhost:19090            ==> hamlib will try to open serial port (BAD).

The problem is that until recently, the last option worked when the piHPSDR backend was still TCP-only, so some users might get frustrated why things don't work that used to work.

Alternative:
========

Of course one could consider an improved "fallback" mechanism in src/rig.c (line 636ff) which falls back to TCP also in the case we have in the input box (aka rigport.pathname) strings like

localhost:19090
my.machine.com:19090

This then would also apply to all other "serial rigs" which are connected via TCP so other users might benefit as well (I know that TS-2000 is frequently used over TCP).
Please check this, but to me It seems this would solve the problem addressed by John and at the same time eliminate the headache (new machine model) of Mike so might be worth considering.

Hi Mike,

WSJT-X always sends a PTT off request on exit as a safety measure, it ignores any errors there. All other invocations should be correctly sequenced as I don't think it is possible to cancel a CAT TX; request from the rig other than turning it off, which would kill the CAT connection anyway. I suppose there may be a race condition where you could turn the rig off an back on without losing CAT control, then an RX command might cause an error. I would not be too concerned about that happening!

I don't think it is reasonable to lie about the rig rejecting a command quite reasonably, just because a client doesn't like it, especially as it may have much deeper consequences.

73
Bill
G4WJS.

The other way I'd prefer to do is ask for PTT status to ensure the RX turned it off and repeat if not.That would in lieu of doing the ID check.

I'm seeing this being stated about the GS-232B and GS-232A protocols:

"Most commands have two versions: one for azimuth, and one for elevation. Commands are not echoed by the Control Interface, but a carriage return character (“0Dh”) is returned after every command, and also a line feed character (“0Ah”) if the command invoked returned data. Invalid commands cause “? >” to be returned and the input buffer cleared."

So basically what should be returned by every command is a carriage return (`0x0D`) and not a line-feed (`0x0A`), unless there is a response from the command.

This means that Hamlib should probably be accepting at least a carriage return (`0x0D`) as a response, but maybe also simply ignore any line feeds (`0x0A`) in order to be extra compatible with all emulations too? I can make the change if it sounds acceptable...

It appears the BKINDL implementation was based on Icom commands which talk in dot length -- so Icom takes into account the CW speed setting and the delay will adjust based on the CW speed setting.
Yaesu thinks in ms and this was apparently not implemented correctly in hamlib.
dot=dit and the setting is 10ths of a dot so a minimum BKINDL to avoid relay clicking would be 3 dots = 3*10 = 30 for Icom rigs regardless of CW speed.
For Yaesu and other rigs we'll need to query the CW keying speed to compute the ms for the dit length.
P = di da da di = 1 1 3 1 3 1 1 (3) = 14 elements
A = di da = 1 1 3 (3) = 8 elements
R = di da di = 1 1 3 1 1 (3) = 10 elements
I = di di = 1 1 1 (3) = 6 elements
S = di di di = 1 1 1 1 1 [7] = 12 elements
Total = 50 elements
() = intercharacter
[] = interword
http://kent-engineers.com/codespeed.htm

So for rigs that need ms we need to read KEYSPD whenever breakin is set or get and compute ms and then to/from dot tenths depending on set or get
I think this will work -- get the keyspd and compute ms-per-dot.    Then we can convert to/from dot tenths.
To read BKINDLY
msperdot = ceil(240*(5.0/KEYSPD)
dot10ths = floor(msfromrig/msperdot)*10
To set BKINDLY
msperdot = ceil(240*(5.0/KEYSPD)
mstorig = msperdot*(dot10ths/10.0)

Right, well -- I think the range of the speed values should be well-defined and the backends should obey the definition. After all, there are only a handful of backends using the speed parameter for anything. Currently, as the speed is defined as 1-100, that's how it should be implemented in each backend -- and that's how I was planning to fix the backends to do it in the upcoming changes. * 0x0d

The flushx conf parameter doesn't seem to be supported on rotctl (but only on rigctl).

However, the post_write_delay seems to be enough to have a reliable workaround for this issue. The K3NG firmware is indeed the reason and doesn't tolerate fast reads after writes -- and it seems to respond with extra terminator chars, but all of this is solved by the delay/flush combination.

I contacted Prosistel and they actually have all the protocol documentation available here: https://www.prosistel.it/download/download.htm

The documentation revealed that there are three "product families", namely the "D" series, the PRO series and the Combi-Track (az+el) combos.

Of these three the D and the PRO series seem to use the same protocol with angle in degrees and A/E identifiers for azimuth and elevation. These rotator controllers support either azimuth or elevation, but not both.

The Combi-Track controllers are combined azimuth+elevation controllers and these represent angles in 1/10ths of degrees *and* use A/B identifiers for unit A and B (which can be thought of as azimuth and elevation).

I've rewritten the backends for Prosistel allowing user to choose between the az, el or az+er models. I'll be able to test the azimuth-only model, so the rest need further testing. I also added support for the stop command.

Hi! The way Frequency control goes for instance in omnirig is to reprogram or change the frequency on the default channel. No need to even name the channel. 
So you connect the radio and send commands. They can be strings or single commands.
Here are the commands 
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hiYPA_Y_1suzQcf1o7-caQ06cyVXURpR/view?usp=drivesdk

If you always use the default channel you will burn out the EEPROM a lot sooner.  That's a fairly old rig and quite possible the EEPROM may not have more then 100,000 writes to any one location.  You'd have to look up the EEPROM model number.
My solution of using channels 441-450 for the 10 bands will minimize the # of writes to EEPROM.  If you work FT8 all day for example you will never have to write to EEPROM.Switching to FT4 will require 1 write and then switching back to FT8 will require another write.  So only when you have to use a different frequency on a band will EEPROM get updated.

> Trying to compile Minos2 and got an error:

>  #include "hamlib/rig.h"

There is a subtle difference between using angle brackets and double
quotes in an #include directive.  In this case,

#include <hamlib/rig.h>

should always be used so the normal system include directories are
searched.

The use of double quotes implies a local header file that is often
located in the same directory as the source file.  Some variables are
set in the Hamlib build system to expand this behavior to to search the
Hamlib source tree but this is not portable to third party software
building against a properly installed Hamlib.

> I havn't been able to find this file - is this a bug in this build? - help please

It should be found in /usr/include/hamlib/rig.h if installed as a system
package in most Linux distributions.  If Hamlib was compiled and
installed locally, then it's probably in /usr/local/include/rig.h.  As
each of these are considered system directories, the C preprocessor
should find it in either location.

Yet here with a set mode command it seems to get it right assumedly 
because the followup ID; query returned a '?;' response. IMHO if a read 
after an 'ID;' command that follows a set command returns a '?;' 
response then we should assume the set command failed, then flush the 
input to skip over any follow up ID response (the whole point of this is 
to avoid a read timeout in the case like this where there is no response 
to teh ID; command), then redo the original set command + ID; sequence 
until retries are exhausted. I am sure that is the way it worked before 
but now it is broken:

it silently carries on without an error, note the sequence:

FT3;  ->
ID;  ->
    -> ?;

does not confirm the FT3; command worked as the response to it is '?;', 
in this case a set command *must* be retried until a follow up 'ID;' 
gives a valid response, or the retires are exhausted; in which case an 
error return from the API call *must* occur.

Yet here with a set mode command it seems to get it right assumedly 
because the followup ID; query returned a '?;' response. IMHO if a read 
after an 'ID;' command that follows a set command returns a '?;' 
response then we should assume the set command failed, then flush the 
input to skip over any follow up ID response (the whole point of this is 
to avoid a read timeout in the case like this where there is no response 
to teh ID; command), then redo the original set command + ID; sequence 
until retries are exhausted. I am sure that is the way it worked before 
but now it is broken:

Hi Mike,

attached is another session using commit 32d5f2b4. The BS commands are 
now a bit better as they are being sent when necessary for VFO A, but no 
attempt to do the required band changes for VFO B. I think this will be 
confusing for owners of Yasesu rigs with dual Rx like the FT-2000 since 
it is not treating the two receivers equally. Surely the logic when a 
frequency change is requested on rigs with a VS command should be:

set VFO X to frequency f:
    use FX; to get the current frequency
    if VFO X current frequency is on a new band:
        use VS; to get the selected VFO
        if selected VFO is not X:
            use VS to select VFO X
        end-if
        send BS command to select new band
        if previously selected VFO was not X:
            use VS to select previous VFO
        end-if
        use FX to set the target frequency on VFO X (could read first to 
avoid redundant change)
    end-if

Other than that the remaining read_string() timeouts are annoying and 
there was a case where 3 retries was not enough, otherwise it seems better.

73
Bill
G4WJS.

I'm thinking of changing the Yaesu and Kenwood retry logic completely.  We're using "ID;" as the verification command.
What would be better would be value verifcation.For example;
Rather thanFA14074000;ID;
We do thisFA14074000;FA;If we don't get the same frequency back in the correct "FA14074000" we repeat after a short timeout....maybe 50ms or so and do 10 triies for around 500ms of effort total.  Higher level retries would still do their thing...this would be it's own internal retry mechanism.  So you wouild still get 3 retries on top of this but highly unlikely to need it.
So all set commands would ask for verification if possible
This would do three things#1 Verifies the command actually worked#2 Eliminates any need for example for ?; response#3 Eliminates long read timeouts as long as the rig is talking at all.

frequency change is requested on rigs with a VS command should be:

set VFO X to frequency f:
    use FX; to get the current frequency
    if VFO X current frequency is on a new band:
        use VS; to get the selected VFO
        if selected VFO is not X:
            use VS to select VFO X
        end-if
        send BS command to select new band
        if previously selected VFO was not X:
            use VS to select previous VFO
        end-if
        use FX to set the target frequency on VFO X (could read first to 
avoid redundant change)
    end-if

Other than that the remaining read_string() timeouts are annoying and

Hi Mikael,

I don't have direct access to the FT-2000 but I believe it works like this.

Press the 'B' button and it goes into VFO B setting mode for 5 seconds. 
While that happens one of the LEDs flashes orange. I would guess the 
VS1; command is doing the same thing and CAT commands for VFO B have to 
be sent within that 5 second period.

I believe the flashing ANT 1 on the display is a reminder that it is the 
VFO B aerial, assumedly for Tx, as the selected Rx aerial is common to 
VFO A and VFO B since the FT-2000 has a single common front end as far 
as the first mixer.

The FTdx500, and FTdx101 as well probably, have genuine independent main 
and sub receivers so may have a different mechanism for the VS command.

73
Bill

I implemented a new retry mechanism.  It tries to validate set commands with the get command to verify that the set actually worked.So we don' really care if what answer we get as we expect to see that the set cmd worked.  Any other answer is just ignored.50ms sleep between each attempt.  May need to be longer like 100ms.  5 tries are done for each command so along with 3 overhead retries give 15 tries taking 750ms+overhead or so worse case.
Let's see how it works.
Mike W9MDB

To my knowledge mobile radios like that do not support CAT control that
Hamlib supports.  Are you sure you're not confusing Chirp with Hamlib?

Software world is Chirp which does memory writes into the EEPROM.

@mdblack98 Thanks, the cache invalidation code seems to fix the issue. Tested on both IC-7300 and IC-7600.

@mdblack98 This is a welcome change. However, I'm thinking if the retries here are unnecessary? They will cause a 3-second delay after a command that fails with an I/O error. Wouldn't a single close/open combination be sufficient? After all, there are retries in the backends too and client using rigctl is able to perform retries accordingly if needed (as it knows the command failed anyway). What I'm after is giving more control of the logic and retries to the client.

Also, is there a real need to have a pause of 1 second between close and open? I'm thinking if a particular radio model needs delays, those should be implemented in the backend. Or maybe a short delay like 50ms could be enough?

It's only on a hard error which should hardly ever occur -- but does -- seen lots of report of com port burps, network burps (I see those).
The internal retries are when there is no hard error.   So it will combine with those retries and then put a 3 second attempt to try and reconnect to the rig too.
Needs some testing...but this may solve the com ports that drop out due to RFI and devices that go to sleep and such.

@mdblack98 Digging deeper. I tested locally by removing the code mentioned in my previous comment and it certainly gets rid of errors with levels. However, the underlying reason for these errors seems to be the following:

1) My remote control app is running commands that result in "soft" errors (e.g. get_level for a level that is not implemented by a backend) -- which should be totally OK and not cause any side-effects

2) However, `rigctl_parse` returns a special value `2` in case of *ANY* error, see: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/27192d0c813aa79c6eb09d85077c7a0fae5489e7/tests/rigctl_parse.c#L1735

3) This will cause the rigctld (and plain rigctl too!) to close and re-open the rig, see: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/27192d0c813aa79c6eb09d85077c7a0fae5489e7/tests/rigctld.c#L1092 and https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/27192d0c813aa79c6eb09d85077c7a0fae5489e7/tests/rigctl.c#L621

4) The rigctld network client calling the soft-failing command will be fine, but `rig_open` and `rig_close` will cause issues for any other rigctld clients -- leading to errors during the time the rig is closed.

What I think should be changed (at least) is the return value logic here:

https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/27192d0c813aa79c6eb09d85077c7a0fae5489e7/tests/rigctl_parse.c#L1735

Could we simply do `RETURNFUNC(retcode);` to make the full return code information available for rigctl loops?

@mdblack98 Of course returning the error code breaks the rigctl loops, as they expect certain subset of values only.

I can try to push a fix for this issue the following way:

1) Remove the "magic" return value 2 (if it's not used elsewhere)

2) Add a concept of a soft error, which would include at least error codes "invalid parameter", "function not available" and "function not implemented" -- in these cases the rigctl loop would continue running and NOT try to re-open the rig.

Sounds good?

After more testing, I can confirm that Hamlib with python 3.9 bindings will compile manually on the Mac if the following lines are removed (or commented out) in configure.ac:

dnl Determine whether to link libpython as it is unneeded for Python >= 3.8
## AM_PYTHON_CHECK_VERSION([${PYTHON}], [3.8], [pyver_3_8="yes"], [pyver_3_8="no"])
## AS_IF([test x"${pyver_3_8}" = "xyes"],[
##      PYTHON_LIBS=""
## ])

py3test.py also runs fine!  So it works!

P.S.  If one manually changes configure.ac with a text editor, the following commands are needed to compile Hamlib with python3.9 bindings:

autoreconf --install
./configure --with-python-binding --prefix=/usr/local
make
sudo make install

Then run:
PYTHONPATH=/usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages:$PYTHONPATH   python   bindings/py3test.py

I did not test building Hamlib with Python3.8 bindings using the updated configure.ac.  But given the changes to configure.ac, I am sure it will also build fine.

Please consider deleting the lines above in configure.ac so Mac users can use Macports to install Hamlib with python 3.8 or 3.9 bindings!

semi colon.  Example Converse Mode command : FA;

Sending ID; in Command Mode will fail to return the ID, even if a 
carriage return and Line feed is included.  It appears rigctl may not be 
appending a carriage return with the ID command.

I thinking this could be done on another port.
So you'd send a command to rigctld to tell it what port to put the audio stream on.  Do we need TCP or UDP?
rigctld would spawn a thread to service audio to that port.

AFAIK the stream that Icom provides is not audio, it's the FFT "buckets" delivered as small, fragmented CI-V packets. The format looks rather generic, but I'm thinking if Hamlib should have its own abstraction over it just to standardize the format rigctld provides. Other manufacturers may provide something similar, I'd need to have a look.

Regarding whether to use TCP or UDP... I'm not sure yet. A TCP server would probably be most straightforward to implement, but UDP would allow higher data rates (for future purposes). However, I think a TCP server might still be the correct choices as the rigctld server should not really care about where it sends the data IMO. With UDP it should be configured to send the data to a particular address, which gets more complicated.

I'm thinking multicast UDP.
Also planning on doing another UDP multicast port of rig information....freq, mode, ptt, width.  So other apps can just listen for updates rather than polling.

That could work. I guess the ports for these could be preconfigured on command line just like the TCP server port. Would there be any need for dynamic port definition? After all, this is all for a specific radio.

Diving a bit deeper into the features.

The following rigs are able to send waterfall data over serial port (or Ethernet/WLAN if the rig has the connection):

- Icom IC-7300 -> Serial only
- Icom IC-7610 -> Serial + Ethernet
- Icom IC-7850/IC-7851 -> Serial + Ethernet
- Icom IC-9700 -> Serial + Ethernet
- Icom IC-R8600 -> Serial + Ethernet
- Icom IC-705 -> Serial + WLAN
- Kenwood TS-890S -> Serial + Ethernet
- Kenwood TS-990S -> Serial + Ethernet

The Ethernet/WLAN connectivity seems to allow faster update rates on the rigs where its available.

The following rigs are able to send wide-band (> 1 MHz bandwidth) I/Q data over Ethernet:

- Icom IC-7610
- Icom IC-R8600

All of the Icom rigs (at least) also seem to offer "IF output" via the USB audio codec instead of the normal audio signal. However, I'm not sure if the data is actually raw I/Q data or something else.

Also, some ideas regarding the broadcast packet contents:

1. It's probably worth introducing a packet/data type field right from day 1, so that it's possible to broadcast other types of (or more extended) data than just get_rig_info. I think this multicast infrastructure could eventually support all transceive type features from rigs, so that any parameter/setting change (RIT/XIT/levels/etc) could be delivered automatically to clients.
2. Regarding the current proposal in JSON format: the VFOs could be represented in a JSON array. Having indexes in JSON key strings is a bit suboptimal IMO.
3. For rigs that do not support transceive, Hamlib could potentially be set up to do internal polling to avoid the current model where the clients have to poll rigs.
4. I see this could be extended to rotctl and ampctl too. At least many rotator controllers do already support reporting their status automatically without queries.

@mdblack98 Ok, so I did some testing on my IC-7300 during the weekend and found out how the Icom waterfall data output works.

With the serial port connection, the following settings must be present in the radio settings:
* baud rate has to be the maximum of 115 200 bps
* `CI-V USB Port` must be set to `Unlink from [REMOTE]`

There are two commands that need to be executed to switch on waterfall output:

`27 10 01` - Switch scope ON
`27 11 01` - Switch ON waterfall data output

The latter command will cause the rig to start *pushing* waterfall data to the controller continuously.

The data is split into small ~50-byte-parts with the serial connection (probably to allow interleaved commands and responses - I guess), but with rigs that have Ethernet/WLAN the data is pushed in a single frame.

For IC-7300 the data is split in 11 parts with the first part containing only metadata, e.g. frequency / span info, and the total number of waterfall data bytes is 475. The number of FFT bins (data points) will vary between rigs and it seems really to depend on the screen size: e.g. 7300 and 705 have the same data length (475 bytes = 475 pixels), but 7610 has more (689 bytes = 689 pixels).

The incoming data is identified by the response command `27 00` so that command is used only as a response, not as a way to poll the waterfall data.

It's also worth noting that the data is *not* sent to the CI-V broadcast address (it's not transceive data).

An example snippet of the data, first frame starts at `*`:

```
                         *
000008c0: 0000 0000 00fd fefe e094 2700 0001 1100  ..........'.....
000008d0: 0090 6903 0000 5002 0000 00fd fefe e094  ..i...P.........
000008e0: 2700 0002 1100 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000  '...............
000008f0: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0700 0000  ................
00000900: 0000 0000 0000 0300 0000 0000 0000 0005  ................
00000910: 0000 0000 0000 00fd fefe e094 2700 0003  ............'...
```

This is all to say that we need to be able to handle push-type data to implement this. The multicast server and the `decode_event` type of transceive functionality need to be present here. It looks like the `set_trn` functionality that uses `decode_event` functions, such as `icom_decode_event`, is already in place -- and hopefully already works.

We will simply need to extend `icom_decode_event` to handle the command `27 00` as a special case of transceive type data -- in addition to the regular broadcast CI-V frames. We'll probably need another type of rig callback for the waterfall data, which would the allow the data to be piped to the UDP multicast server eventually. I'm thinking we can create a simple abstraction of the waterfall frames based on Icom's specs. I'll have a look at what kind of waterfall data Kenwood rigs provide, but IIRC it's very similar. The waterfall frames would include the frequency / span info in addition to some normalized, 8-bit waterfall data = FFT buckets that are evenly spaced.

Thoughts?

@mdblack98 This is an initial spec for spectrum data I wrote down quickly based on both Icom and Kenwood rig manuals:

# Spectrum data content

```
SpectrumLength=475
SpectrumData=00AAFF75BD2AAA ...
SpectrumDataMinLevel=0
SpectrumDataMaxLevel=140
SpectrumDataMinStrength=-100
SpectrumDataMaxStrength=0
```

`SpectrumLength`: Number of bytes in `SpectrumData`. Not strictly required, but helps verifying the data is complete.

`SpectrumData`: 8-bit data in Hex ASCII format.

`SpectrumDataMinLevel`: The value that represents the minimum signal level. This may change depending on the settings of the rig -- at least on Kenwood the subscope provides different kind of data comparted to the main scope.

`SpectrumDataMaxLevel`: The value that represents the maximum signal level. This may change depending on the settings of the rig -- at least on Kenwood the subscope provides different kind of data comparted to the main scope.

`SpectrumDataMinStrength`: The strength of the minimun signal level in dB. This may change depending on the settings of the rig -- at least on Kenwood the subscope provides different kind of data comparted to the main scope. The level values are assumed to represent the dB strength scale in a linear way.

`SpectrumDataMinStrength`: The strength of the maximum signal level in dB. This may change depending on the settings of the rig -- at least on Kenwood the subscope provides different kind of data comparted to the main scope. The level values are assumed to represent the dB strength scale in a linear way.

# Spectrum types

`SpectrumType`: Icom has additional modes SCROLL-F and SCROLL-C to allow scrolling past the boundaries of the screen and have the spectrum flip over to the corresponding area/"page", but the SCROLL modes can be mapped to these. We can have extlevel to set the Icom-specific modes. Kenwood rigs seem to have the same options, excluding SCROLL-C, but it looks like fixed mode edges for Kenwood are more freely specifiable.
```
SpectrumType=FIXED|CENTER 
```

## Spectrum type: CENTER

If `SpectrumType=CENTER`, the following fields will be present:

```
SpectrumCenterFreq=14267000
SpectrumSpan=25000
```

## Spectrum type: FIXED

If `SpectrumType=FIXED`, the following fields will be present:

```
SpectrumLowFreq=14000000
SpectrumHighFreq=14250000
```

In JSON format this could be:

```
{
  "Spectrum": {
    "Length": 475,
    "Data": "00AAFF75BD2AAA ...",
    "Type": "FIXED|CENTER",
    "MinLevel": 0,
    "MaxLevel": 140,
    "MinStrength": -100,
    "MaxStrength": 0,

    // If Type=CENTER, the following fields will be present:
    "CenterFreq": 14267000,
    "Span": 25000,
    
    // If SpectrumType=FIXED, the following fields will be present:
    "LowFreq": 14000000,
    "HighFreq": 14250000
  }
}
```

@mdblack98 Yes, the example is mostly based on real values. The indices (bins) in the spectrum data will not map exactly to any integer frequencies. The data received from the rig is most likely subject to some kind of averaging anyway, since it seems to depend on the screen size (as that's what the manual says), so the rig outputs what the rig displays on the screen.

The spectrum data lengths are:

* IC-7300 / IC-9700 / IC-705 / IC-R8600: 475 bytes (bins)
* IC-7610 / IC-785x: 689 bytes (bins)

The data ranges (bin values) are:

* IC-7300 / IC-9700 / IC-705 / IC-R8600: 0-160
* IC-7610  / IC-785x: 0-200 (at least on newer firmware, older manual says 0-136 for IC-785x)

The scope span settings in center mode are for all rigs:

* 2.5k, 5k, 10k, 25k, 50k, 100k, 250k, 500k

* IC-R8600 supports also: 1000k and 2500k

In fixed mode, the scope span will vary, it can even be the whole band.

Kenwood TS-890S:
* Main scope: 32 * 20 bytes = 640 bytes (bins)
* Sub scope: 12 * 19 bytes = 228 bytes (bins)
* Kenwood also specifies the signal levels:
  * Main scope: 00h = 0dB, 8Ch = -100dB
  * Sub scope: 00h = 0dB, 32h = -50dB


Kenwood TS-990S:
* Main scope: 32 * 20 bytes = 640 bytes (bins)
* Sub scope: 15 * 19 bytes = 285 bytes (bins)
* Kenwood also specifies the signal levels:
  * Main scope: 00h = 0dB, 8Ch = -100dB
  * Sub scope: 00h = 0dB, 32h = -50dB

I'm not sure if it is possible to find at least some approximations on the signal levels for Icoms. There are some markings on the screen waterfall display regarding dB scale.

@mdblack98 I could already start adding some code to parse the spectrum data in the Icom backend, handling it in `icom_decode_event`. 

I think we could do the following changes:

1. Add a spectrum data callback to `rig_callbacks`: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/master/include/hamlib/rig.h#L2304 -- so that direct Hamlib API usage of the data is possible. Spectrum data will need its own struct for metadata and a buffer for the actual FFT data.
2. I guess rigctld can the directly use this callback (and all the other callbacks too for transceive use) with the multicast server to cache and deliver data updates via the multicast UDP packets. The existing callbacks seem to be used only in `rigctl_parse.c` simply printing out the (change of) data.
3. One more challenge is the passing of spectrum data from rig backend to the callback, as we're talking about frequent (minimum of multiple times per second) delivery of ~500-1000 bytes of data. Allocating/freeing data dynamically doesn't sound like a good option. I'm thinking of creating some sort of simple pre-allocated buffer pool for this purpose. The buffer pool would be allocated by the rig backend and the spectrum data struct/buffer would be valid during the callback. I guess that should be enough as the callback should really push out the spectrum data as a UDP packet as soon as possible.

Comments?

Also, some comments about the multicast data format:

* There are some inconsistencies between the text token format and JSON: The format don't have the same fields, e.g. PTT and Status and ErrorMsg are missing in JSON. Also, the field Seq is only present in JSON.
* I'm not sure if we really need the Seq number, as there's not much the receiving end can do if a packet is missing. Regarding spectrum data usage, I could possibly imagine the receiver application could wait for a *very* short time (in the order of under 100ms) for any out-of-order packets to arrive. Though I do see the Seq number as an indicator for missing/out-of-order data, as even with localhost delivery the ordering of UDP packets is never guaranteed.
* Let's keep the field names and the naming convention consistent between the formats. If we go for the field names starting with a capital letter (to preserve the existing convention in other Hamlib field names), `vfos` should probably be `VFOs` or `Vfos`.

@mdblack98 Regarding the multicast data content, should all the messages include all of the fields or simply the data that gets updated at that time? I'm thinking of the latter, otherwise we'd need to cache all the data, which doesn't work for the spectrum data.

I would **_very_** strongly recommend the use of Semantic Versioning for this protocol, and its representation(s). This will give you a great deal of flexibility in defining compatibility levels and degrees of change, and allow implementations / clients to determine how much or how little they can support. Date-based versioning gives you **_no_** flexibility, since a client needs to treat every date change as if it were a major change, even if it was in fact a tiny change. See https://semver.org/ for details, if you're unfamiliar with Semantic Versioning.

The following method is the same as the method used for the ARCP-990 bandscope.

 

1) Determine whether the current status is Center Mode or Fixed Mode by using the "BS3"command.

 

2)In case of Center Mode

Add or subtract the RIT/XIT frequency ("RF" command) to the MAIN Band frequency ("FA" command) or SUB Band frequency ("FB" command) to obtain the actual current center frequency.

Then add or subtract the SPAN frequency obtained by the "BS4" command to the center frequency to calculate the lower and upper frequencies of the bandscope.

 

3) In case of Fixed Mode

Directly obtain the lower and upper frequencies of the bandscope using the "BS5" command.

 

4)Calculate each spectral frequency by dividing the area between the lower and upper frequencies by 640.

Hi all,

master at commit a0672e4f has regressed, it no longer reliably sets the split Tx VFO frequency as requested by a set_split_freq_mode(). Note that in the first (failing) example below the SUB VFO is never selected even though the MAIN VFO is selected no less than six times while attempting to execute this command! The end result is that the requested SPLIT Tx VFO frequency is set on the MAIN Rx VFO.

Note also the second trace output below where in the same session set_split_freq_mode() does manage to set the right frequency in the right VFO, rather inconistent behaviour!

I was wondering about the assumption a rig back end can make on the rig pointer being !null.
I see some code that assume rig != NULL, while other code adds actual checks. Either not checking is a bug or checking is redundant.

Running a simple grep on check for rig pointer not being NULL:
grep -R '!rig[^_-]' --include=*.[ch] rigs
shows most older Yaesu rigs have checks for every possible function, most other rigs have no check or only one. Most check only in the close function.

I think all these check are (no longer?) required. I expect these should only be accessed via the API which could check this.

I am willing to code this cleanup, but I first wanted to know what the policy is.

Dropping backend checks will expose missing front end checks sooner; a crash is easier spotted then an error return.
I think your example is flawed:
```
rig.c: 
 
rig_set_vfo(rig) //rig is local memory
 icom_set_vfo(rig)
     --do some funky code that corrupts the **memory pointed to** by rig. It cannot destroy rig 
 icom_set(rig) //rig is local still local
    --rig is still valid (not NULL). The **memory pointed to** is corrupted. So the null check is not helping.
```
Once again, I do not see how adding NULL checks on every call is even remotely helping. 
Let alone it justifies the effort to implement, maintain and test the huge amount of extra code.

There are very little checks currently so I think the current API is doing proper checks already.
Using tools like valgrind or AddressSanitizer are a way more efficient approach to find memory corruption.

That was my point about improving the check to look for a valid pointer instead of just NULL.That would be useful.
So if you want to change anything follow my recommendation to make it a macro/function combo and we'll improve the function then which will apply it everywhere.

It's put in for future rigctld use.The problem is particularly bad for non-vfo mode where setting freq can be like this.
V VFOBF 14074000V VFOA
If another rigctld client wants VFOA freq it will do this which could be done in the middle of the 1st sequence without any control.  V VFOAf

This is really a mutex but I didn't want to call it that.  It's only meant for a short time -- 1 second right now which should cover most situations so doesn't quite qualify as a mutex.  A cookie implies expiring.

rigctld has no way of knowing that multiple commands are occurring or that another client is running so this is a solution to this potential problem.  In hamlib 5.0 this may be forced....haven't decided yet.  Nobody has reported a problem with this but the new mulitcast ability is going to aggravate this condition.  Hamlib will be polling the rig asynchronously soon which it's never done before.

I think I understand what rig_cookie is trying to achieve: implement some sort of locking to allow multi-threaded applications.
But I think there are some serious issues;
   
   - Locking is only done when having pthread, so if that is not enabled there is no multi thread guarantee.
   - Even if pthread is available the lock should also be used when reading cookie to protect against writes, not just when setting.
   - The lock should also protect timestamp.
   - Fetching timestamp should be done AFTER getting the lock. otherwise significant time could have past waiting for the lock.

To me it really seems like a problem that should be solved at the application layer. Why is hamlib trying to provide this? Are there any known users?
