I don't think we want to put a mutex in there as the only solution.  The idea of a cookie is if it gets refused then you can do other things before asking again or just skip the request....e.g. inside a wait loop or such rather than getting stuck on the mutex request.
This cookie idea would be implemented in hamlib 5.0 so that no request could come in without holding the cookie.
Another possibility is to use the mutex if a cookie has not (ever) been requested by the client -- that would provide backwards compatibility and could be implemented in hamlib 4.4.
This approach might also allow multiple clients to talk to one serial port if we can make all operations atomic.  So another client opening the serial port would get a fake OK.  Sounds possible.

The mutex is for doing an cookie operation nothing else.
So thread A gets the mutex and then starts a get operation. Thread B will have to wait a little before thread A is done with grabbing the cookie. But after that short while it will run and gets the result the cookie is taken already. And it can do what ever it wants.
For the cookie to work properly the access on cookie and the timestamp needs to be atomic. That is fixed by the lock.
Also note that for the "cookie get" command the mutex usage did not change. I did not intend to change any logic flow with regard to the mutex.

We're going to need a bunch more locks...inside every rig_ function in rig.c unique to each function.But this is a good start to help keep things thread safe.
There's one area I know is not thread safe and that's the debug msgs.  It's a global buffer right now so could be clobbered by threading.  Not likely to happen as retreiving debug should be very fast compared to any rig actions but with the new caching that will be happening due to the multicast it will be more likely.

I think we have avoided this for so long as even though authentication is reasonably straightforward, adding encryption looks like staring into the abyss to me!

I've preferred to direct those who needs such things to SSH as it handles authentication in a secure manner--password or public key--and encryption.  Add to that its tunneling capabilities and it takes care of all we need.  What we don't have is a guide to setting up SSH to be used in this manner.  Examples abound on the Internet but sometimes key details are mixed up.  More advanced use involves reverse tunnels which I have setup to my AllStar repeater so that as long as it can get an outbound network connection it will contact a host in my LAN (firewall port opened, etc.) and set up the tunnel.  On that host I can make a connection to `locahost:port` and be connected.

Just some thoughts.

The need for encryption is way overblown.
Right now there's no security at all so there is a potential hole for any remote connection -- even if done via port redirection which I know some do.A simple password solves 99.9999% of problems -- no encryption needed -- and I'm going to use a self-generated password so it is pseudo-random and users don't reuse some common password.
So it will be something like this:
rigctld --set-passwordpassword: XXXXXXXXThen add a --use-password XXXXXXX option that expects a certain format as rigctld provides. 
So yes...if somebody happens to monitoring the packets the password is in clear text...but nob ody is doing that between a ham operator and their remote rig.  But an open port is subject to scanning.

I'm working on a radio GUI and just find this issue with my FT-991A (connected via rigctld).
By rig CAT manual, should be possible to read/write separately VFOA and B, CAT command FA and FB. But hamlib 4.3 supports only current VFO. Please update the frontend.

Some notes: the 991 has a single receiver and the current VFO is always the VFOA, the VFOB is used only to trasmit when in split mode. When VFO swap function is used, the focus doesn't change from one VFO to another as other radio models, but as said before, A becames B and viceversa, so the active VFO is only VFOA.

OH...and from rigctld you need to add the --vfo option to the command line so you can send the vfo with the command.
f VFOA 14074000
f VFOB 14075000
m VFOA USB -1
m VFOB USB -1
The -1 means no passband change.

I suppose we could add a "virtual VFO" to the 991 -- we've done that in other places where the rig is fixed and it's just for the API like rigctld so it does not need the --vfo argument.

The rig is actually SDR Console over a virtual com port - it presents itself as a TS-2000.

It might not be DNS but can't think what else it is. If I run the same test locally (i.e. from localhost) there's no issue at all (returns within a few milliseconds) so it's not the 'rig' side of things.

If I use SparkSDR (which implements its own version of rigctld) it's also fine over the network. The network itself isn't the issue, it's something that rigctld on Windows is doing.

The order of events as I understand it from what I've tested is:

1. TCP connection successfully established
2. rigctld tries to get the hostname of the source connection (this is the bit I'd like to try disabling)
3. 4.5 second delay (possibly trying some windows specific methods of lookup?)
4. PTR DNS request recieved by nameserver
5. DNS response sent/recieved (within 1.3ms)
6. rigctl logs: Connection opened from rpi4:36714
6. command recieved and processed ('get frequency')
7. reply is sent
8. TCP session closes
9. rigctl logs: Connection closed from rpi4:36714

The fact rigctl logs 'rpi4:36714' means it's translated the source address to 'rpi4' otherwise I'd expect to see '192.168.9.35:36714'.

The PTR request is of course the standard way of doing lookups so I'm wondering if windows is trying some proprietary lookup nonsense before it resorts to a PTR lookup.

I assume rigctl is using a standard library to perform the hostname resoluition of the source address - I believe it's something in there causing the delay. I would question why rigctl even cares what the hostname of the source request is.

For rigs that don't have a way to directly set VFOB mode you will see split turn off, VFOB activated, VFOB mode set, VFOA activated, split turned on again.
I'm think about not querying VFOB mode and using the cached value to determine if it should change.  That would mean if the user makes a mode change on VFOB they are on their own and hamlib won't change it back until a restart.  But it would avoid all the display flashing that's occurring now on different rigs.

Are you 100% sure it's not CI-V? I've used `socat` on a Linux machine to connect a TCP listen socket to a radio's CI-V port, then told RS-BA1 to connect to that port, and it worked.

Yes, there's some other stuff, including a discovery protocol over UDP, and a separate protocol for the remote audio, but I believe that the CAT aspect of it is 100% just CI-V over TCP.

That said, I don't have a radio with the builtin ethernet (7610, 9700, or 705) to test things out from the client end :)

Hamlib does not have a UDP interface so perhaps could add that and give it a try.

Like I've mentioned above, the Kappanhang project has a working implementation of the Icom network protocol.

The protocol seems to use separate UDP ports for different streams (control/auth, serial, audio) and the CI-V commands are wrapped inside UDP frames:

Control: https://github.com/nonoo/kappanhang/blob/main/controlstream.go#L41

Serial: https://github.com/nonoo/kappanhang/blob/main/serialstream.go#L33

In a way Kappanhang could used *with* (Linux only, of course) Hamlib as it seems to use loopback serial and audio devices to expose the radio connection.

This could be implemented in Hamlib too, but it requires quite a lot of logic -- and to be useful Hamlib should probably have a way to transfer audio to and from the device. Maybe through raw UDP audio streams?

This does require the RS_BA software to be running, right?
Or does the rig itself does support this?

The if condition for whether there actually is a second port is only
covering the sprintf for the elevation command, and not the write
attempt. So we call rotorez_send_priv_cmd2 whether rotport2 is valid or
not. When it's not, we try to write the command to fd 0 (stdin). When
running on the console, this results in trash on the console. When
runnning under something else (e.g. systemd) this results in errors or
other wierd behavior (e.g. EBADF because stdin isn't connected, causing
the command to fail with RIG_EIO).

As of 2020-01-19 changing offset frequencies is muting VFO-A.

Doing VSO; or VS1; when rig is already on that VFO causes the VFO to mute.
So had to change rig_set_vfo to check the VFO first.

After pulling & recompiling if I try set_vfo_opt(0) I now get an error:

```
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Input In [8], in <module>
----> 1 my_rig.set_vfo_opt(0)

TypeError: set_vfo_opt() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
```

In icom.c:

- If `icom_get_usb_echo_off()` and/or `rig_get_freq()` fail in `icom_rig_open()`, it will simply make rig_open fail on line: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/be992b8a36a999726306f0214d847bbadd6587ea/rigs/icom/icom.c#L1008 -- this has changed during the recent echo off check code refactoring.

- Additionally, rigctld will not accept failing `rig_open()` initially, but will do `exit(2)` on line: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/be992b8a36a999726306f0214d847bbadd6587ea/tests/rigctld.c#L697

  - This has not changed in a long time, but we could basically allow rig_open() to fail and let the "main handler loop" for clients handle rig_open() / rig_close() like it does now.

@mdblack98 I'm already working on some improvements to rigctld.c (e.g. locking rig_open/rig_close), so I can try to fix this if we just agree how.

My proposal would be to:

1) Allow `icom_rig_open()` in `icom.c` to succeed after 1 retry of getting echo off / frequency, but probably with `priv->poweron = 0`.

2) Remove the `exit(2)` in `rigctld.c` in case `rig_open()` fails -- or potentially have a conf setting to allow this. We can move `rig_opened` to a global variable and have it reflect the initial result of `rig_open()`, so that the client handler will re-attempt opening.

I can push out a PR soon about this proposal.

I don't think we need #1.  #2 sounds OK as long as priv->poweron = 0.  If they are asking for the rig to power-on at startup and it fails it should fail hard.

Did you add yourself to the dialout group?

In order to run some of the commands featured on this website, you will need to give yourself sudo access, and add yourself to the dialout group. This applies to the primary machine, and any virtual machines running CentOS / Fedora. If you install VirtualBox to run virtualised images, you will also need to add your uid to the vboxusers group.

Open a terminal window and enter: su - to become super-user. You will be prompted for your root password.

Add yourself to the wheel and dialout groups with the following command: usermod -G wheel,dialout uid
- where uid is your id as found from the command: whoami.

In the same terminal window as above, edit /etc/sudoers and un-comment either of the %wheel options, depending on whether you want to input your password each time you run a sudo command, or not. I prefer not, so I un-comment: %wheel    ALL=(ALL)    NOPASSWD: ALL

You will need to log-out and log-in again for the above changes to take effect.

Rig command: W ID; 6
Reply: ID900;

Can also do hexadecimal

Rig command: W \0x49\0x44\0x3b 6
Reply: ID900;

int rig_send_raw(rig, unsigned char *send, int send_len, unsigned char *reply, int reply_len, unsigned char term);
send contains the raw command data
send_len is the # of bytes to send
If reply is NULL no answer is expected
reply should be as long as need for any reply
term is the command termination char -- could be semicolon, CR, or 0xfd for Icom rigs

As part of our university project I created a simple HAMLIB backend for the GOMSPACE GS100 transceiver. New backend allows changing and reading RX and TX frequency using the f/F and the i/I commands, which is practical for setting up and remote control the RIG and for Doppler compensation. Problem

When rigctl connects to TS-950SDX the frequency from the information readout IF matches the displayed frequency on the radio, but in contrast when FA or FB (get_freq) is issued the response does not match the displayed frequency. set_freq does not set the frequency on the radio display.

How to reproduce
   
   - connect rigctl to TS-950SDX by rigctl --model=2013 --rig-file=/dev/ttyUSB0 -vvvvv
   - send IF command: W IF; 38      
      - receive: IF00014070030

   - send FA command: W FA; 14      
      - receive FA00007074000, expect IF00014070030

   - send FB command: W FB; 14      
      - receive FB00010136000, expect IF00014070030


What I tried
   
   - Deactivated cache; behaviour did not change:
   cache_timeout: "Cache timeout, value of 0 disables caching"
	Default: 500, Value: 500
   	Range: 0.0..5000.0, step 1.0
   
   - Exactly specified the connection parameters; behaviour did not change:   
rigctl --model=2013 --rig-file=/dev/ttyUSB0 --dcd-type=RIG --serial-speed=4800 --set-conf=stop_bits=2,serial_parity=None,serial_handshake=Hardware,data_bits=8 -vvvvv
   - Configured grig, flrig or wsjtx or so that the frequency/band of the radio can be changed by software.

   - Tried with TS-950SDX settings "Transfr" (allows data transfer between two TS-950SDX) and "Direct" (whether signals are directly written to VFO by Transfr function or not) in all variants (all off, all on, only Transfr, only Direct).

This is the second attempt at PR #1022, please confirm it works for you.

Gentoo issue: https://bugs.gentoo.org/798273

When building hamlib with --with-tcl-binding and slibtool (https://dev.midipix.org/cross/slibtool) it will fail with many undefined references for tcl.

This is because the TCL_LIBS is never set correctly and it uses -no-undefined during the build. GNU libtool does not reveal this problem because it will silently ignore -no-undefined. This patch will use PKG_CHECK_MODULES to find the linker flags and sets them where needed.

The difference with the original PR is that instead of an error when tcl.pc is not found it will then check for tclConfig.sh instead. I also added an error for when the SC_LOAD_TCLCONFIG macro fails to load the config file in case both the pkgconfig file and tclConfig.sh are missing while the tcl.h header is present.

Took me less than I anticipated. The result is it mostly works however there are some non conformances between the rig behaviour and programming reference.

The CAT description says:
```
COMMAND: *RMNN<noise_reduction_value><CR>
< noise_reduction_value > = ON/OFF Selection / level
0 = Noise Reduction Off
1..9 = Noise Reduction ON and at the specified level

QUERY: ?RMNN<CR>
Examples: PC Query Eagle Response Meaning
?RMNN<CR> @RMNA7<CR> Noise Reduction on level 7
?RMNN<CR> @RMNA0<CR> Noise Reduction off
```

However, the rig behaves differently. The NR level can be set from the front panel between 1..10. When reading ?RMNN the response is @RMNN0 for NR off, and @RMNN1 to **@RMNN10** for NR on with appropriate level.

Sending *RMNN0 disables NR. NR symbol is not shown on the front panel. However, when NR button is pressed, NR symbol appears but the NR itself does not work. Sending ?RMNN returns @RMNN0. Small imperfection but who cares.

Sending *RMNN1-9 correctly sets NR level and enables it.

Sending *RMNN10 sets NR level 1. This is both confirmed via front panel and also via ?RMNN command. I guess the rig does not handle two characters in level number.

I would suggest to:
1. Assume 10 levels for NR and change the code accordingly ( /9.0 and *9.0 change to 10.0 in set_level and get_level)
2. Get NR level will correctly return the NR level between 0.0 (off) and 1.0 (level 10 set)
3. Setting the NR level will work correctly between values 0.0 (off) and 0.9 (level 9).
4. Level 10 will not be settable via CAT interface due to a bug in the rigs firmware

I guess 4. is not going to be an issue. This whole NR settings is not used very often.

Try another pull...I think it should behave now...level 9 will set level 9 and should return 0.9 for the value.Level 10 manual set on the rig should return 1.0.

@mdblack98 I discovered the cause of the bouncing CTRL + PTT.

At the moment, the rig_caps of TMD710.c has:
`.targetable_vfo =  RIG_TARGETABLE_NONE,`
but should be:
`.targetable_vfo = RIG_TARGETABLE_FREQ,`

As I understand it, this specifies that the rig can get/set frequencies without needing to set control to that VFO.

Because of this, every time a different VFO is operated on (to get/set frequency etc),  eg. rig_(get|set)_freq (rig.c) calls set_vfo, which sets the CTRL+ PTT to the target VFO.  This is unnecessary as these rigs don't need control to operate on the frequencies.

.targetable_vfo = RIG_TARGETABLE_NONE,
but should be:
.targetable_vfo = RIG_TARGETABLE_FREQ,

As I understand it, this specifies that the rig can get/set frequencies without needing to set control to that VFO.

Because of this, every time a different VFO is operated on (to get/set frequency etc), eg. rig_(get|set)_freq (rig.c) calls set_vfo, which sets the CTRL+ PTT to the target VFO. This is unnecessary as these rigs don't need control to operate on the frequencies.

That's because every OS sadly has a different standard for this. As someone who's had to deal with this for work, here are the standards:

 - [Linux](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/basedir-spec-latest.html): somewhere in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, falling back to ~/.config
 - Windows: %APPDATA%.
 - [MacOS](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/FileManagement/Conceptual/FileSystemProgrammingGuide/FileSystemOverview/FileSystemOverview.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/TP40010672-CH2-SW1): "~/Library/Application Support".
 - [Android](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/app-specific): Context.getFilesDir(). You also have getExternalFilesDir, which is user accessible but might be on a removable card.
 - Other platforms: ???

Messy? Yes it is. Naturally, a lot of apps either predated the many standards or wanted One Thing To Rule All Platforms, so they added a hidden file/dir (dot-prefix = hidden for mac/linux) in the home directory. That works everywhere except maybe android.

Calling rig_set_split_freq when split is not turned on has several possibilities.  I believe the intent was that it would not be called if split was not on.

The current vfo is what will transmit if split is not on -- the function probably should have been called rig_set_tx_freq but you will get that effect if you use RIG_VFO_TX as the vfo in the function call.

There are several ways to treat this....

#1 If split is not on set the current vfo (as that is the TX vfo at this state of the rig) -- current behavior
#2 If split is not on return an error
#3 If split is not on set the vfo requested
#4 If split is not on set the TX vfo (which takes current vfo into account) and ignore the requested vfo -- this is reverse split if you then turn split on after this.

I think the current behavior is the best  as you can just call this function with RIG_VFO_TX and whatever the TX vfo is will get set.

Now the problem comes in when the VFO gets selected for some rigs as that changes the split direction and why this function takes that into account.

I think the current behavior is the best we can get.

One should be able to do this

rig_set_split(rig, RIG_VFO_A, 1, RIG_VFO_B);  // set split as you want it
rig_set_freq(rig, RIG_VFO_RX, freq);
rig_set_freq(rig, RIG_VFO_TX, splitfreq);

I believe that should work on all rigs now as VFO_A/B are mapped to whatever the rig uses (e.g. Main/Sub)

I hate to be rude but you've come barging into the project yesterday without introduction proclaiming we're wrong when the project has followed the Best Practices outlined by the Gnu Project and the Gnu Autotools project for _decades_.  The documentation is correct for the way this project is structured and maintained.  While I think Mike's addition to the INSTALL file is not necessary I am willing to leave it be as he wrote it.

Unlike other projects you may have encountered, Hamlib's Git repository is not distribution ready nor is it ready to simply compile and go.  The reasons are many and technical but a quick summary is that not just the `configure` script but several support files are required as well.  These files will change depending on what version of Autotools was used to generate them.  Someone on Debian is going to have a different set of files from someone on Arch, and for anyone developing on MinGW they will all be different yet again.  That is just for Autoconf, Automake requires all of the `Makefile.in`s be present and `libtool` has its own pile of files it needs present and all of those can vary depending on the Autotools version and whatever patches a distribution has applied.  It just isn't logical to maintain a project of this scope will all of the build system files changing from developer to developer.  If we didn't do it the way we do applying a simple patch from one developer to the next would be a nightmare.

What you fail to understand is that `bootstrap` is not included in a release tarball nor should it.  The `README` and `INSTALL` files are included in the source tarball as are others for completeness, but those two are required by Autotools to create a release source tarball and are intended to only explain what is needed to build Hamlib from that release source tarball.  I invite you to compare the files contained in the latest daily source tarball available from https://n0nb.users.sourceforge.net/ found in the first section titled, "Hamlib Git master branch source snapshot" to what you find in the Git repository.  We intend for the Git repository to be a source only archive containing no files generated by the build system.

I hope this explanation is useful.

1. \power2mW seems to work ok now
2. \get_level still reports very coarse power information

It is using "PC" to get the current power level which gives the KX2 responds with anything between "PC000;" (near zero/zero power) and "PC010;" (10W).  This is not enough precision to be able to calculate the power accurately in \power2mW.

Here's a sampling of what happens.  KX2 power setting -> \get_level value -> \power2mW result:

* 10W -> 0.666667 -> 10W
* 9.8W -> 0.600000 -> 9W
* 9.0W -> 0.600000 -> 9W
* 6.6W -> 0.400000 -> 6W
* 6.0W -> 0.400000 -> 6W
* 1.0W -> 0.066667 -> 1W
* 0.9W -> 0.000000 -> 0W

This is all the precision that the standard PC format offers, but the Elecraft doc suggests that the "K2 extended mode" gives 0.1W resolution instead of just 1W resolution.  The doc says:

> K2 Extended RSP format (K22): PCnnnx; where nnn is power, and x is 0 (low range) or 1 (high range). Notes: (1) A lower power limit may be in effect on trasnsverter bands (menu entries X V TR 1-9). (3) The MN and DS command can be used to select other settings of the KPA3 MD menu parameter.

Earlier, the manual describes the K22 mode as:

> K22, K2 Extended mode: Enables all K2 command extensions.

At least skimming through the manual, it looks like it should be safe to enable the extended mode on rig open and then interpret the PC value appropriately.  However, for all I know there are assumptions in some of the other Kenwood/Elecraft rig code that'd trip up on possible changes in FW, ID, and KY behavior.

I'm not sure if I misunderstood you, or you misunderstood me.  So, just to make sure, let me try to rephrase.

On FreeBSD, OS-provided external software ("ports") are installed in /usr/local.  The base system (kernel, basic userspace) is in /usr.  (On Linux, both are in /usr.)

I run into *build errors* because CPPFLAGS includes -I/usr/local/include *before* -I../include.  This makes the compiler find rig.h from the installed binary package instead of finding rig.h in the source tree I'm trying to compile.

Any software's build system should use its own headers in the source tree instead of using same-named headers in /usr/include or /usr/local/include.  In other words, this is *not* about /usr/local/include vs. /usr/include, but rather about ${path-to-hamlib-source}/include vs. /usr/local/include.

We should be able to put in a test for /usr/include/hamlib/rig.h and die with a message like:

"Do not install a 2nd hamlib version.  You should uninstall the system hamlib package first".

This is actually a major problem with Linux versions (or any Unix really) as any apps that are compiled with a prior version will cease to work when libhamlib.so is replaced.  Windows can put the DLL in the directory so upgrading Hamlib won't break Windows applications.  Linux versions are also prohibited from static linking so that can't be done either.

I'm thinking we need to migrate to a different include path using the major version (compatibility indicator) and also include the major/minor version on the libraries too.

Seems the shared library versions should also show the full version number which they don't now.

That's because the rig cannot return PS status when it is turned off so we have to assume power is on.  A timeout does not necessarily mean power is off.  Some rigs can return power status when turned off.

Does this cause a problem with some software package?

I think that assuming RIG_POWER_ON when there is a timeout of the get_powerstat command, it's not logic.
It generates an indetermination and will be not possible to understand if the rig is really on, off or there is a communication delay or error.

Did you try the latest master?  It might be getting power status now when power is off.

WSJT-X utilizes Hamlib for it's cat control middleware and Hamlib expects the 9700 to be at the default address of A2. This huge PR removes some unused includes and adds some includes needed for correctness or clarity following some of the suggestions of the tool "Include What You use".

Removing config.h where not needed is a strong hint that a source file is portable.

7. As you can see, rigctld receives the request from the client, convert the command get_power_stat, send it to the radio (Yaesu PS;) and receive the right answer (PS0;) but for some reason doesn't send the information to the client.
8. Rigctld continue to send commands to the radio in a kind of loop after the client is disconnected for the timeout, I have to stop it by forcing with Ctrl+C.

You need to start rigctld with auto_power_on otherwise it will never try to auto start the rig.
You can also use the -Y switch on rigctl to have it continue even though it gets errors.

After looking at this, I think it's actually working (at least mostly?) as expected:

1) Note that this test case is about a missing serial port and *not* about rig being powered off (but serial port still being present).

2) rigctld (the daemon) will automatically close any client connection when it cannot open a rig. It will try to open the rig 1+3 times and then give up and close the rigctl client connection.

3) rigctl (the client using netrigctl backend) simply detects closing of the connection, fails and exits.

4) If the --ignore-err (or -Y) option is given to rigctl (the client), it will stay accepting commands and after any command it will cause rigctld (the daemon) to try to reopen the rig. If that fails, it will again detect closing of the connection, getting an I/O error (-6) internally from rig_open(). However, the resulting error code from rigctl (the client) is Invalid parameter (-1), since any command, such as rig_get_freq(), will return EINVAL error code if the rig is not open.

@mdblack98 Any comments on which of these are not correct behavior? After all, I think that if the serial port doesn't exist, rigctl error codes should reflect that and NOT indicate that power is off.

P.S. Regarding the other bug with rigctl client in netrigctl not following auto_power_on (or auto_power_off) is a simple fix, since automatic power on/off is not global behavior in rig.c (not 100% sure if it could be -- some rigs may need special handling in rig_open before commands can be supplied). I will push out a PR regarding those fixes soon.

Sounds like RFI Problems due to noise on the USB cable


Tests
If problems are occurring only during transmit:
    #1 Reduce power to zero and see if the problem stops -- if it does stop than it is definitely RFI.  You will see certain higher power levels on certain bands that cause problems.
Then, if problems are occurring during non-transmit periods it indicates a system problem with USB devices so...
    #1 Check USB Power Management option is turned off on all USB devices
        Device Manager for Windows.
        For Linux set autosuspend=-1 https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/usb/power-management.html


RFI Fixes:
    #1 Free - Move USB cables to another port -- some ports are more susceptible than others.
    #2 Free -- Check your grounding system.  rod-outside-the-shack is a common problem when it's not bonded to the main house ground. 
        Common grounding mistakes, sources, and solutions:
        A. Ground rod outside the shack that is not bonded to the main house ground.
        B. Shack equipment bonded incorrectly (e.g. daisy chained instead of common ground point)
        C. Desktop computer grounded to the house ground and not the shack ground.  Run a separate RF ground from the computer chassis to your station RF ground.
           For a laptop use the retaining screw of a DB9 or DB25 connector shell, if your device still has them.
        D. Ethernet cables that bring RFI into the computer...which then ends up going to the rig too since the ethernet shield is tied to the case which is tied to USB shield which is tied to pin 4 on the USB cable (a very common problem on most all USB devices -- see my QRZ page).
           Ethernet patch cables up through CAT6 are UTP, which stands for UNSHIELDED Twisted Pairs, four to be specific.  There is NO separate shield conductor in the jacket, nor a metallic shield around the RJ45 connector itself.
           Just use a ferrite toroid at each end.
        E. Wall warts -- 24VAC supplies in sprinkler and alarm systems are notorious for picking up RFI into your electrical system.
           24 VAC transformers can be RF-bypassed using .005 ufd caps from each output lead to safety ground. You can often use the cover plate mounting screw as your ground connection.
        F. Speaker wires The same approach as E also works for external speaker audio leads.
        G. Lamps (yes...lamps around the house have unshielded wires as do many other appliances).
        H. Washer/Dryers are notorious for generating and picking up RFI.  In general, newer high-efficiency models have more RF problems.  
           Ferrite toroids INSIDE the appliance housing can work wonders if the wiring harness has connectors in the AC line input, OR an external noise filter for the AC line cord of a washing machine can reduce RF spurs by 25 dB or more.
        I. HVAC systems with variable speed blower control systems both cause RF noise and react badly to RF fields -- we believe adding torroids inside the unit on the power lines will work.
        J. If you use a powered USB expansion hub, add a ferrite toroid on the cable coming from the USB power supply.
        K. SignaLink -- You can ground the metal box shell by simply wrapping an 18ga wire (or use a small crimped ring or spade terminal) under the head of any of the screws holding the rear panel, then connect to your station RF ground. 
           The case is isolated from both USB and analog audio signal grounds, so this does not affect use of the USB shield isolators.
        L. DC power supply -- both linear and switching -- READ THE PS MANUAL FIRST!  This step may void some manufacturers' warranty and UL/CSA approvals. 
           Remove any jumpers between the DC negative output lead and PS chassis or line cord ground  Add a .005 ufd cap from each DC output lead to chassis ground if not already there. 
           NOTE: Samlex DC outputs are already isolated and bypassed, but many others, including Astron, may randomly have the negative side grounded and no RF bypassing. 
        B through L may all need chokes.    
        http://www.k9yc.com/GroundingAndAudio.pdf 
    #3 Free -- start unplugging devices around the house and see if there's one device that is acting as a bad source of RFI.  This presupposes you can easily repeat the problem on your rig setup.
    #4 Cheap -- Add some USB shield isolators (see my QRZ page).  I use one on my SignaLink for example.
    #5 Minimal $$ -- Good USB cables like this
    https://www.amazon.ca/Tripp-U023-006-Device-Ferrite-Chokes/dp/B003MQ29B2/ref=sr_1_5?crid=11YRNPWDVWGCU&keywords=usb+cable+with+choke&qid=1658187349&sprefix=usb+cable+with+choke%2Caps%2C139&sr=8-5
    #6 Maybe free (if you have chokes...otherwise can get a bit costly) -- add chokes to USB cables first, then all other cables including power, ethernet, and control cables.
    Fair-Rite torroids are good quality -- do NOT buy cheap Chinese ones --  https://www.fair-rite.com/product/toroids-5943003801/  You can use clip-ons but torroids allow multiple wraps and give better results.
    https://www.fair-rite.com/product/round-cable-snap-its-431176451/
    I couldn't find type 31 torroids at Fair-Rite as of 20220721 but Palomar has some palomar-engineers.com/ferrite-products/ferrite-cores/ferrite-ring-toroid-combo-pack/
    Newark also carries them https://newark.com/c/passive-components/emc-rfi-suppression/ferrites-ferrite-assortments?brand=fair-rite

I have an MD-01 controller running firmware version 2.0.237 that is connected to the computer via the COM0 DB9 port. When it receives a control command to move the rotator, it prints debug logs to the serial output that look like this:
input:
  W3600\x0A4500\x0A\x2F\x20

output:
  W\x03\x06\x00\x00\x0A\x04\x05\x01\x00\x0A\x20
  287925671: in motion\r\n
  287925673: Change motion state M0 to mcsStart\r\n
  287925678: GO  A 0.000000 0.000000 t ---\r\n
  287925680: in motion\r\n
  287925683: Change motion state M1 to mcsStart\r\n
  287925686: GO  E 90.000000 91.000000 t ---\r\n
  287925690: distance to go M0 too small. End.\r\n
  287925694: Change motion state M0 to mcsStopped\r\n
  287925698: Stop on motor 0 on angle 0.000000\r\n
  287925703: Change motion state M1 to mcsRunning\r\n
  287926610: distance to go M1 too small. End.\r\n
  287926613: Change motion state M1 to mcsStopped\r\n
  287926617: Stop on motor 1 on angle 90.000000\r\n

Note that the response frame is not necessarily present in an specific order relative to the log messages: I have seen it come after the logs as well. Because the current implementation just slurps up response bytes without checking the framing or anything, as soon as any of this log data enters the command stream, all subsequent commands will read completely bogus responses.

Regardless of whether it's due to a misconfiguration, a weird artifact of the firmware, or something more sinister, the MD-01 is awkwardly interspersing its normal fixed-size-frame response with these line-based log messages. As shown above, the log messages appear to be consistently of the format <timestamp>: <message>\r\n, where <timestamp> is some kind of integer timestamp (possibly relative to unit boot) and <message> is an ASCII string.

Due to poor(?) design decisions by the protocol designers, the frame start and end bytes are both printable ASCII characters ('W' and ' ' respectively) and the MD-01 response frame contains no other validation information (such as a CRC), which means that a valid log line could fairly easily contain a character sequence that is indistinguishable from a valid response frame, without actually being a valid response frame.

However, since the log messages appear to be reasonably strictly structured, we can make a small number of assumptions that will allow us to reliably separate response frames from log lines without having to fall back on a heuristic-based parsing strategy. These assumptions are as follows:

     
    1. A log line will always begin with an ASCII character in the range [0-9], none of which are the frame start byte.
    
    2. A log line will never contain \r\n in the middle of the line (i.e. multi-line log messages do not exist). This means a log "frame" will always be of the form [0-9]<anything>\r\n.
    
    3. The controller will not emit a response frame in the middle of a log line.
    
    4. The operating system's serial port read buffer is large enough that we won't lose data while accumulating log messages between commands.
    

Provided the above assumptions are true, a simple state machine can be used to parse the response by treating the log lines as a different type of frame. This could be made much more robust by applying additional heuristics for specific packets (e.g. get_position has some reasonably strict numerical bounds that could be used to sanity check the contents of the reply frame).

I was finally able to sit down and test this today and it works with the MD-01 I have that produces log messages on `COM 0`. However, it's worth noting that both `COM 1` and the `USB` serial port do not appear to have log messages printed to them, so physically plugging the serial cable into a different port on the device is an alternative fix to this problem.

I do generally think that this change improves the robustness of the SPID implementation, but I understand it's also very difficult to regression test such a change without a variety of hardware/firmware combinations. All I can say on that front is that it fixed the problems I was having using `rotctl` directly. My testing was performed manually on the CLI and was certainly not exhaustive.

Here's the executive summary of the changes I made:

- When reading data that does not start with `W`, which is the ROT2PROG frame start byte, the reader will repeatedly consume data until it receives the CRLF (`\r\n`) newline sequence until it finds a valid `W`.
- Some log messages do not start with a timestamp, such as when the `MD-01` is reconfigured with the serial session open, as mentioned in the second commit.
- The 3rd commit adds flushing the serial read buffer before every write, which seems to do a very good job of keeping the read stream free of log data in general. It's possible that this commit on its own largely addresses the problem, but:
   - I don't know if flushing the read buffer has performance implications for writing
   - I only tested this typing into the CLI, so it's entirely likely that this solution may not be sufficient when commanding at high speed over a socket, etc.

The problem is mainly with Icom as we don't know the active VFO of any Icom rig.  The current VFO is always RX and the "other" VFO is transmit.   So we have some choices....but we need to be able to support  reverse  split on everybody.

This includes  Main/Sub rigs who can run split either way too but still can't figure out what VFO is active.  Icom rigs in sat mode can only transmit on Sub which is what you see in the Icom code if VFO_TX is the targeted mode or  VFO_SUB is the transmit based on the original split setup.
So before you do anything let's be clear about what you think ought to happen.

Also current_vfo=RX is only true if not transmitting as I believe all Icom rigs show the split VFO active during transmit.
So, if we try to change frequency for Doppler control need allow that too.

set_split_vfo
    #1 Should use vfo_tx argument to determine TX vfo, vfo is ignored.  Should return an error if TX vfo cannot be done...not there are cases where  Main/Sub is restriced on which can transmit.

set_split_freq/set_split_mode/set_split_freq_mode

Ok, do you have any more information on what is going wrong? Maybe I can help.

The way the multicast routines work is that they are *completely* independent from any rig control. They have their own pipe that is used to push data to be published via multicast packets.

So it cannot directly interfere with reading of frequencies or anything.

NOTE!!! That said, if there is something wrong with the Windows-based pipes (I remember it was painful to set them up), things could go wrong. But the reason is the pipe setup then.

Also, to be frank, none of this rig cache-related stuff should be here in the publisher routine -- it should not contain any references to rig data access directly: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/commit/541c1e1de23cc41e020546b8bce4cf00a773f822#diff-5db0914fb2aeac80a2dd975e05ef91ee9367ea525c46c3ce128d1670b5eca4aaR926

Instead, there are already functions you can call to trigger publishing a new state snapshot packet, see this:

* The `network_publish_rig_poll_data` function is used to indicate that polling was used to detect a change: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/325277f269615eef8fdfb1fc1104203557dc99b1/src/network.c#L741
* The `network_publish_rig_transceive_data` function is used to indicate that async/transceive updates were used to detect a change: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/325277f269615eef8fdfb1fc1104203557dc99b1/src/network.c#L761

Both of them actually lead to the same result: publishing of the snapshot data packet.

I'm looking here that you wish to poll data from rig to publish updates. There is already some code ready for this purpose, but I never got to testing it really. The poll routine is here, but it is somewhat incomplete and needs a bit of work to detect all changes correctly:

https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/325277f269615eef8fdfb1fc1104203557dc99b1/src/event.c#L69

It *could* use the cache as well instead of actively reading from rig!

There are also start/stop functions for the poll routine, but they are not really called anywhere (at least not unless enabled):

https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/325277f269615eef8fdfb1fc1104203557dc99b1/src/event.c#L251

^ That's probably something you wish to do set up as well, right?

One more note about checking when the multicast routines stop -- this type of polling of any "stop indicator" should *not* be needed: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/commit/9b6d1565f137b8f0a61b9c934d1c0eded866e9fd#diff-79c406beb22c5bf0c5eedc5f0343a87c6eb434ae6de6171b493e44a18ff43e2cR1545 -- the `network_multicast_publisher_stop` function *joins* the thread and waits for it to stop, see here: https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/commit/9b6d1565f137b8f0a61b9c934d1c0eded866e9fd#diff-5db0914fb2aeac80a2dd975e05ef91ee9367ea525c46c3ce128d1670b5eca4aaR1128

It's the polling that's the problem.

Since the audio data is async it's interlaced with other packets.

The multicast I put in does not poll yet and relies on a client to do frequency polling or setting and is why it uses the cache.
We need to put a mutex in to control who is running a transaction on the rig so they don't collide.
Hamlib expects sync control for rig control (guaranteed response to requests) and the async ability on top of that  is a bit of a kludge as you well know.

One of the problems I ran into was the multicast running the doing the read() was timing out when async was not enabled.
Also was seeing a segfault in WSJT-X (only through the debugger) at shutdown so there was an attempt to fix which may still be around and not needed now.

@mdblack98 I think I found a way to make this all work on both Linux and Windows. The workaround is to:

1) Use `INADDR_ANY` when binding (in Windows only) and just subscribing to the multicast group. However, this still allows other traffic like unicast to be received, but rigctl can just ignore any message it doesn't recognize.

2) Use a different port for the multicast commands (multicast receiver) to not consume the multicast state updates / spectrum data sent to port 4532.

It seems that on Windows one cannot bind sockets directly to multicast group addresses. This should be supported -- although discouraged -- based on the official MS documentation here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock/nf-winsock-bind#remarks

> For multicast operations, the preferred method is to call the bind function to associate a socket with a local IP address and then join the multicast group. Although this order of operations is not mandatory, it is strongly recommended. So a multicast application would first select an IPv4 or IPv6 address on the local computer, the wildcard IPv4 address (INADDR_ANY), or the wildcard IPv6 address (in6addr_any). The the multicast application would then call the bind function with this address in the in the sa_data member of the name parameter to associate the local IP address with the socket. If a wildcard address was specified, then Windows will select the local IP address to use. 

However, in practice the bind() calls seem to fail when trying to bind to a multicast address, see:

* https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6140734/cannot-bind-to-multicast-address-windows
* https://cygwin.cygwin.narkive.com/gcVdp3ce/bind-to-multicast-address-fails

So on Windows we'd use the workaround to bind to `INADDR_ANY`.

So far, initial testing on IC-7300 has been successful, with no VFO swapping -- now, when the rig advertises TARGETABLE_FREQ and/or TARGETABLE_MODE, apps like loggers can easily poll/read *AND change* both the VFOA/VFOB frequencies and also the split freq/mode without VFO swapping. Reverse split with VFOA as TX vfo seems to work too. I will test with older rigs too (have an IC-7600 and IC-756Pro3 available too). Obviously, the older rigs (without 0x25/0x26 commands) still need VFO swapping if polling actively or changing opposite VFO freq/mode.

The UDP multicast will of course make polling unnecessary in the future -- once apps adopt it!

A small question to you though: I saw that you had been working on improving IC-9700 support (mainly the VFO selection) this year. That is all working and clear to me how it works, but did you ever test whether the 0x25/0x26 commands could read the SUB receiver freq/mode? To me it looks like those commands only read the MAIN receiver VFO (when not in satellite mode). That is very confusing. Selecting the SUB receiver using the CI-V command or by tapping the screen doesn't affect the 0x25/0x26 results at all.

Maybe the "old-style" freq get/set commands 0x03 and 0x05 are the only ones that are able to set the SUB receiver freq?

@mdblack98 This is already implemented in the Icom backend (requires async mode to be enabled) and works -- as long as Hamlib can track the current VFO (-> user doesn't change VFO from the rig buttons). Not sure if there is anything else one can do to make it better, because of the CI-V limitations.

@mdblack98 The multicast state data published by Hamlib is getting ready for initial testing.

 I also did test the UDP multicast on both Windows and Linux with an IC-7300 with async+spectrum output enabled and it seems to work very well! The UDP packet with spectrum data and the "regular" state updates get nicely interleaved. I also tested running multiple UDP listeners and multiple rigctl instances simultaneously and it all works also on Windows. Looks promising.

This particular GitHub issue seems to cover quite a lot of things, both multicast state data publishing AND control commands. Now we have the state snapshot data packet publishing almost ready and some groundwork done for listening for commands.

I propose this issue could be closed and a new issue be opened for the rig CONTROL commands -- it doesn't have any spec regarding the command format and how they would work either. Probably something not going to be implemented for 4.6 either :)

Any remaining bugs/features for the state snapshot data packets can be created as separate issues, right?

Also tagging related multicast work PRs already merge here:

IC706 is 1 stop-bit -- but that should not be the problem.
You can shorten up your line and just let it use the defaults and add -vvv to see errors/warnings

rigctld -m 3011 -r /dev/ttyUSB0 --set-conf=dtr_state=OFF,rts_state=ON -vvv
Could be your serial cable may want dtr_state ON but that would  typically be for an older USB cable.
Try this and see what it says...
rigctld -m 3011 -r /dev/ttyUSB0 -vvv

I understand very well how it works - I've been working with shared code/unique data since the early/mid 1970s[1].  It's not the multiple programs that doesn't work - it is one program with different hamlibs.

Let's see if I can make up an example.  Suppose we have a program (compiled against 4.5.5 or 4.6) that is happily connected to a rig via hamlib (4.5.5 or 4.6).  The program decides to change mode to one where the timeouts and retries are taking too long.  So it sets rig->state.pttport.retry, and rig->state.pttport.timeout to new, smaller values, and gets faster notice of problems so it can adapt.

Now that same program (same binary) runs again with a new hamlib (4.7/5.0) that has the pointerized pttport.  The program sets the same values into the same (now deprecated) memory, but the hamlib in use isn't looking at those locations for its operating parameters.  So that same old program no longer functions as it did.

Granted, this is not the normal use case.  Most changes to pttport are essentially config changes, done before rig_open(), or are done via rig_set_conf(), and they can be copied into the new struct. So this may or may not be a problem in the real world.

And that's why I think that at some point in the (maybe far distant) future we should do a full reset of the ABI, and clear away the accumulated cruft of the last 20+ years. 

[1] Whenever Sperry-Univac implemented ER LINK$|ER EXLINK$ on Exec 8

If running the latest WSJT-X (rc4) there's a Hamlib update in the rig tab.
Otherwise new hamlib for installation directions
#1 Shut down WSJTX 
#2 Download either the 32-bit or 64-bit DLL matching the 32/64-bit version of WSJTX -- hopefully your browser doesn't block it but may warn you multiple times.
If you can do a "Save As" you can save it directly in the appropriate WSJTX directoryC:\WSJT\WSJTX\bin and replace the libhamlib-4.dll that is there.
http://n0nb.users.sourceforge.net/dll32/libhamlib-4.dll
http://n0nb.users.sourceforge.net/dll64/libhamlib-4.dll
Linux/Unix/Mac users need to compile the latest tar file from http://n0nb.users.sourceforge.netNote: If compiling on Unix-like systems please uninstall any Hamlib package you have before installing the new build
#3 If you don't save directly you need to open a file browser and move the file that way.
If you're not familiar with that here's a video on the file browser - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AyVqCJrs9dk
Once installed on Linux do "ldconfig".
rigctl --version should then show a relatively recent date of the download
Mike W9MDB

This is all handled by the PTT line going into an amplifier that does not get asserted until the sequencer tells it to.
But...WSJT-X needs to have a delay also on sending the audio -- as it has no idea when PTT actually gets asserted.

Not sure we need to disable the PTT on the rig while doing this.  And Hamlib doesn't know it's an Arduino connected so DTR blocking really isn't feasible....other than no DTR/RTS if using CAT commands perhaps...make them exclusive.

Mike,

Some further comments although at the moment I don’t see a real benefit to add serial mode PTT signaling to the “second” USB connection for PTT.

 

> Not sure we need to disable the PTT on the rig while doing this.

#3 What I want to achieve is a single PTT control on the rig. For that reason there should not be any PTT related CAT commands to the rig via the current CAT connection. The new serial connection should do all PTT control to sequencer. 

The next issue is how reliable that serial connection should be. Currently it is a signal RTS or DTR. I have no knowledge, whether wsjt-x tries to check that the PTT signal has activated transmission on before starting to send audio; perhaps after the delay defined in wsjt-x Settings | Advanced | TX delay: setting. 

If there is no checking that rig is ready to accept audio (only a delay), then I think that your protocol proposal #3 is an overkill. I assume that the reliability of the serial communication should be high enough and we don’t need to check whether the sequencer got the message. The only need for the polling TX could be, if the sequencer can indicate that now the audio can be sent and HamLib can tell that to wsjt-x. 

By the way does any rig give an indication that a PTT action for transmission is completed? If so, is it a response message or does HamLib do it by polling?

 

#4 and #6 Sure we can leave for operator to select in wsjt-x RTS for PTT and not DTR in the case of Arduino. Of course we could change wsjt-x MMI, e.g. RTS, DTR and CAT(TX), but that may not be needed at the end.

#8 As Joe W4TV clearly pointed this enhancement request is only a software correction to a missing RTS wire in Arduino. Personally I still can do soldering although hands a shaking and would just add the missing wire!

 

#9 Another possibility is Sam’s proposal that the sequencer does all this and takes the full CAT control and delivers to rig other CAT commands directly and catch PTT issues and deliver those only after completing sequencing. Best solution unless sequencer can accept RTS signal.

 

73, Reino OH3mA

OK...so here's what I think the "best" solution is.

A generic function in rig.c that can save parameter setting (both conf item and value)
A generic function in rig.c that can process that list given a port.

Backends that need to wait for _open then determine in the set_conf if the device is open and, if not, queue the conf=XXX string.
Backends then look for the queue in the _open call and process it.

Then this is just a few lines in each backend that needs it -- and actually the same few lines in them.

"Plus you missed saving the value which is used for the command selection in the set_conf function."

This gets me the most - I save the command that would be sent to the rotator, not anything from the set_conf call.  It's already been encoded with the value - upper case for set, lower case for clear.   I just send the same command to the rotator a little bit later.

"Turns our rotorez is not the only one that does this and it is much simpler to handle this in rotctl/rotctld with a 1-line change to add a rotor then to put this code in every backend."

Yes, it might be simpler - but wrong.  It doesn't fix the root cause, that rotorez_set_conf() doesn't agree with the (unwritten) Hamlib specifications.  That means an application(not just rotctl[d]) will call rot_set_conf() before rot_open(), expecting the value will be set for future use, whenever it is referenced.  Moreover, it could mix frontend and backend parameters in the same set of calls.  They have to be handled similarly. 


ISTM that this is the very basic reason that Hamlib exists - to provide a completely consistent sequence of calls to handle any parameter of any device.

If there are others, I'll fix those too.  Why? Because I don't like incomplete fixes. It only took half an hour to write the code once I figured out where things were, so lets fix it right.

The idea I gave can also support any X=Y setting for conf or parm settings for example.

I have a Guohe PMR-171, which uses almost same command set with Guohe Q900. The frame format is totally different with quite simple FT-817 style 5-byte command, but a frame with 4-byte long header, variable length and CRC. I haven't look into the whole repo yet, but I think there is some rig using similar frame structure and we may build upon it.
Guohe protocol makes use of several advanced feature. For example, we can set VFO A and B's freq in one frame and no need to switch VFO A/B which needs to adjust filters while making noises (especially satellite ops). I would like to see it as soon as possible...

That makes things a bit slow. I could also switch to rigctld, does that make more sense?

You can ignore regressions if you have a system that doesn't have an API used by other applications. However, if you are implementing a library where different versions are distributed across various distributions, this unfortunately cannot be overlooked. That's my opinion. If you want to improve the debug output, perfect, every positive improvement is welcome, but it has to be accompanied by a note somewhere stating that this API has changed or by using a different function name. For example, the Qt library constantly changes something, but each release is accompanied by a list of all the public API changes, so library users know what to expect. Hamlib isn't released that often, so this should be possible to create. This way, each application can adapt before users start reporting issues.

My comment regarding open/close was just rhetorical. It's not relevant to this discussion. Look, I don't want to create an unfriendly environment here. Open-source projects should cooperate. But you also have to think about the projects that use your product and what impact it might have on them.

There is no API for the debug output.  I've tried to standardize some things but it is not intended to be parsed by anything.  And I don't know of anybody trying to parse it.

One issue I find, though, is that the scan is forced to be on VFOA.  It doesn't matter which VFO I'm on, the radio is forcibly moved to VFOA before the scan starts.  This is true even if I put both a VFO change and a scan together on the same line ("V VFOB g VFO 0").

I'm not sure that this makes sense.  I understand that the radio won't report which VFO it's on, so Hamlib can't be 100% confident which type of scan it's doing unless it changes to a specific VFO.  But it's certainly unexpected to have it switch away from VFOB when you ask for a VFO scan.

I think I also understand the issue with the mismatch between the interface Hamlib provides and what ICOM CI-V is providing.  The Hamlib scan request specifies a scan on a specific type of VFO, either VFO or MEM, and CI-V only has a single command:  start a scan on the current VFO, no matter the type.

There might be a straightforward way to address this, however.  Instead of Hamlib using the CI-V command to explicitly change to a specific VFO (Command:  0x07 Subcommand:  0x00), why not use the CI-V command that returns to the last used VFO (Command 0x07 **no** subcommand)?  From my testing, that works correctly whether the radio is in MEM mode or currently in a VFO.  For MEM mode, it returns to the last-used VFO.  For VFOA/VFOB, it does nothing.

I tested with raw CI-V commands:  the radio will indeed perform a VFO scan while in VFO B.  And when paired with the switch-to-last-used-VFO command seems to give consistent and intuitive results.

In any case, thank you very much for all of your help!  At least the basic function is at least somewhat possible now, if limited to VFOA.

I just went digging a bit into icom.c to figure out how the scan command is being sent.  Turns out I was looking at a slightly older version.  I found the commit that fixed scan operation for the IC-707:  https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/commit/baf2897e76b367325a1a2085df7bf4b0459fd862  Glad I decided to try the latest just in case!  :)

It seems that the VFOA switch is indeed hard-coded into the icom.c icom_scan() function now (line 8681):  `retval = rig_set_vfo(rig, scan==RIG_SCAN_MEM?RIG_VFO_MEM:RIG_VFO_A);`  It seems what we need is something like a "RIG_VFO_LAST" using the 0x07 CI-V command without a subcommand, instead of forcing "RIG_VFO_A".

A little more exploring and I found where the VFO change subcommand parameters are coded:  icom_defs.h starting at line 151.  Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be an option for no subcommand, at least not there.

Looking around the icom.c/h code, I don't really see any concept of being able to specify "last VFO":  it always seems to be hard-coded as VFOA or VFOB (usually A).  But it seems all we need is a way to specify a RIG_VFO_LAST that will execute the 0x07 command without subcommand and use that instead of RIG_VFO_A in that line in icom.c.

I know, easy for me to say:  I'm not doing the work!  :)

If adding the idea of "last VFO" would be too difficult, would it be possible to make the ICOM scan commands a two-part command?  If the "scan MEM" command were a 0x08 (switch to MEM) command followed by the 0x0e 0x01 (start scan) command, and the "scan VFO" command were a 0x07 (switch to last VFO) / 0x0e 0x01 (start scan).  Then icom_scan() wouldn't have to explicitly change VFO at all -- let the radio do the work! :)

I'm pretty certain you need **none** of this information -- I'm sure you know Hamlib and CI-V **way** better than I.  But I wanted to record what I found at least for myself, so I thought I'd add it here to keep it all in one place.

Again, thank you **very** much for all of your efforts!  The IC-707 is really so much more useful with Hamlib, and I'm grateful for the cleanup effort on such an old and little-used radio.

```
.chan_list =  {
        {   1,  25, RIG_MTYPE_MEM, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP },
        {  26,  30, RIG_MTYPE_SPLIT, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP },    /* split ? */
        {  31,  32, RIG_MTYPE_EDGE, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP },
        RIG_CHAN_END,
    },
```

There's only two places in the codebase where "RIG_MTYPE_SPLIT" is used:  ic707.c above and rig.h:
```
typedef enum {
    RIG_MTYPE_NONE =    0,  /*!< None */
    RIG_MTYPE_MEM,          /*!< Regular */
    RIG_MTYPE_EDGE,         /*!< Scan edge */
    RIG_MTYPE_CALL,         /*!< Call channel */
    RIG_MTYPE_MEMOPAD,      /*!< Memory pad */
    RIG_MTYPE_SAT,          /*!< Satellite */
    RIG_MTYPE_BAND,         /*!< VFO/Band channel */
    RIG_MTYPE_PRIO,         /*!< Priority channel */
	RIG_MTYPE_VOICE,		/*!< Stored Voice Message */
	RIG_MTYPE_MORSE,		/*!< Morse Message */
	RIG_MTYPE_SPLIT			/*!< Split operations */
} chan_type_t;
```

Interesting that only the IC-707 code uses the SPLIT mem cap:  I would have thought that this would have been more common?  And this code all predates my interest in the IC-707, so I'm not sure what motivated this to be added only for it.

In any case, with more digging, there's another area it seems where memory channel capabilities need to be defined.  /src/misc.c:
```
static const struct
{
    chan_type_t mtype;
    const char *str;
} mtype_str[] =
{
    { RIG_MTYPE_MEM, "MEM" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_EDGE, "EDGE" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_CALL, "CALL" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_MEMOPAD, "MEMOPAD" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_SAT, "SAT" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_BAND, "BAND" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_PRIO, "PRIO" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_NONE, "" },
};
```

It seems that RIG_MTYPE_SPLIT isn't in that list, and that's why there isn't a more specific tag for channels 26-30.

I thought it was odd that only the IC-707 has memory channels marked as SPLIT.  For example, a quick check of the IC-737 shows that it **too** has single-freq and split/dual-freq memories (PDF page 40 of the manual).  So does the IC-725/726/728/729.  I checked the IC-706 manual:  it seems by then that the rigs were upgraded so all memories were split memories.

Given that there are a few (but only a few) rigs that have these different types of memory, maybe it would make sense to mark the **single-freq memories** instead of the split memories?  If most memories are split, and it's a given that all current and new rigs will have all-split memories, why not tag the old and limited memory slots?

So that would be my proposal:  change memory caps in ic707.c:
```
.chan_list =  {
        {   1,  25, RIG_MTYPE_SINGLE, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP }, /* Single-freq memories */
        {  26,  30, RIG_MTYPE_MEM, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP },
        {  31,  32, RIG_MTYPE_EDGE, IC_MIN_MEM_CAP },
        RIG_CHAN_END,
    },
```

Change the SPLIT type to SINGLE in the enum of memory types in rig.h:
```
typedef enum {
    RIG_MTYPE_NONE =    0,  /*!< None */
    RIG_MTYPE_MEM,          /*!< Regular */
    RIG_MTYPE_EDGE,         /*!< Scan edge */
    RIG_MTYPE_CALL,         /*!< Call channel */
    RIG_MTYPE_MEMOPAD,      /*!< Memory pad */
    RIG_MTYPE_SAT,          /*!< Satellite */
    RIG_MTYPE_BAND,         /*!< VFO/Band channel */
    RIG_MTYPE_PRIO,         /*!< Priority channel */
	RIG_MTYPE_VOICE,		/*!< Stored Voice Message */
	RIG_MTYPE_MORSE,		/*!< Morse Message */
	RIG_MTYPE_SINGLE			/*!< Single-freq operations */
} chan_type_t;
```

And add SINGLE to the mtype_str[] struct:
```
static const struct
{
    chan_type_t mtype;
    const char *str;
} mtype_str[] =
{
    { RIG_MTYPE_MEM, "MEM" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_EDGE, "EDGE" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_CALL, "CALL" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_MEMOPAD, "MEMOPAD" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_SAT, "SAT" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_BAND, "BAND" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_PRIO, "PRIO" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_SINGLE, "SINGLE" },
    { RIG_MTYPE_NONE, "" },
};
```

I'm lazy, and I haven't forked Hamlib; but if you want an actual, formal PR just ask and I'm happy to do so.  But you'll probably want to make the changes your own way, anyway.

In case you want to update the models that I found the single/dual memory divisions:  IC-737/765:  memories 1-89 are single, 90-99 are split, and "P1, P2" are edge channels; IC-725/726/728/729:  0-22 singe, 23-24 dual, 25-26 edge.  Oddly enough, the IC-271/471 support 32 memories and all support duplex, with channels 1-2 as edge channels.  I suspect the IC-781/970 only support single-freq memories, but the manual is vague on that.  That's all I've checked.

I'm going to re-open this issue for further visibility and look forward to your thoughts.

Thank you very much for all of your help!

If I select model `Q900`, it will work, but `Q900` entry is defined in `ft817.c` and it is using Guohe's "817 compatible mode". Model `PMR-171`, along with CRC checks, is defined in `pmr171.c` using Guohe's native protocols. I wonder whether others were testing the right model and which firmware version...

I saw in `pmr171.c` line 459 (also line 812 and more) that it took 3 instead of 2 (length byte of 0x03 (counting 2 CRC bytes), and 1 command byte - so it should `len-1`) bytes into CRC16 calculations. After this patch, it passed CRC check on my PMR-171 with latest firmware v3.5.0 released in November 2024. But there're still bugs (freq's are in plain hex, not BCD code like Yaesu rigs, etc.) and I'm working on it.

By the way, according to upgrade notes, PMR-171 firmware v3.5.0 supports controls via UDP. Maybe we can make a new entry for it, in a later time.

/MACHINE

Specifies the target platform for the program. Usually, you don't need to specify /MACHINE. LIB infers the machine type from the .obj files. However, in some circumstances, LIB can't determine the machine type and issues an error message. If such an error occurs, specify /MACHINE. In /EXTRACT mode, this option is for verification only. Use lib /? at the command line to see available machine types.

A 2nd decimal makes things complicated.   I would strip comma and decimals except for the right most decimal.  The sender is assured to supply the value in MHz so that guarantees at least 1 decimal.  Any others to the left become expendable.

Another approach is to strip all commas and all decimals and skip the multiply by 1e6.  The value is 6 digits after the decimal so converts to Hz by itself.

The daily snapshots are generated on a virtual machine here on my desktop around 4 to 4:30 AM Central time and posted to https://n0nb.users.sourceforge.net/  It generates the source archive and also builds the Windows 32 and 64 bit binaries.  Aside from having to download the entire `.ZIP` archive, the 32 and 64 bit `.DLL` files are available separately.  My understanding is that these can be "dropped in" and used for testing the master branch code.  Mike, W9MDB (SK) asked for this capability a couple years back.

The licensing is very intentional.  At one point the library was a mixture of GPLv2/LGPLv2.1 and I went through a lengthy process to contact all contributors of GPLv2 code to agree to relicense to LGPL2.1 which they agreed to.  The reason being that while we wanted to keep the Library as Free Software we did not think it was right to dictate license terms to software developers that want to use Hamlib.  This has allowed software with other licenses to use Hamlib.  I understand that doesn't sit well with Free Software purists but we also have a pragmatic side.

The utilities and such are licensed under the GPLv2, i.e. everything that doesn't go into `libhamlib.so.4.*`

That said, unlike the Linux kernel, we have not struck the *or (at your option) any later version.* clause.  So the code could be relicensed at some future date if such a situation arose, but any new code contributed could not be backward licensed under the current licenses without express consent, as I understand it.

And while Web based use is gaining traction, the main Hamlib library is, as I see it, too low level to be concerned with the AGPL.  Plus the majority of its use is in classic linked into another program on a single user computer fashion and may remain so for some time.  That's not to say that the Hamlib project won't include code that fits better under the AGPL and some work has been moving in that direction.  When that time comes we can consider licensing those necessary parts under the AGPL, assuming it is compatible with the current licenses.

Unfortunately, I've not been as intimate with the project over the past five plus years as I had been prior, but since the death of Mike, W9MDB, last month, I've been stepping back in as time permits.  Since I've been with the project since the beginning of 2001 I thought I should reply with an historical perspective.

I want to close by saying that Hamlib is very much a Free Software project and intends to remain so.  Are we less free by sticking with the older license versions?  Are we at risk?

As I recall, one of the major reasons for the GPL3 is so-called Tivo-ization of Free Software.  Is Hamlib at risk for that?  Perhaps.  Maybe.  Probably.  As I see it, someone inclined to do so isn't likely to be too scared of a lawsuit from a hobbyist project regardless of the license that covers it.  Much of the enforcement of software licenses comes down to what I'll loosely define as Western Morality.  Other cultures and traditions appear to vary in their acceptance of such morality.

I have gotten back to working on this, and even have a dynamically allocated cache version that works with WSJT-X.  However, I made a few changes while deprecating the definitions in rig.h that may need to be discussed.

The definition in rig.h was changed from 'struct rig_cache' to 'struct rig_cache_deprecated', and the references in rig_state changed likewise.   However, the new definition went into src/cache.h, not include/hamlib/rig.h - out of scope for any application compiled with Hamlib.

I did this for several reasons -
- My general dislike for having active internal data shared between library and application - how the cached operations are really done is not germane to the app, only to Hamlib.
- Current programming practice - let the object manage its own data, without outside meddling.
- Having another albatross around the necks of current and future Hamlib developers.  See how much code was needed to handle previous deprecations, and even then compatibility is only in one direction.
- And the big technical reason - if Hamlib is ever going to handle rigs sending state changes automatically (Auto Information in Kenwood-speak), then the whole idea of cache needs to change.  STATE(rig) should always be up to date, commands sent to the rig are confirmed automatically, inquiries should have the requested data already available; cache may not even be involved.

Since I don't have a feel for what applications are doing with current cache data, I'm really looking for feedback on how to proceed.  Do I need to provide some sort of bridge to/from the old cache structure; are changes to the API necessary; or do I start over?  Should I start a discussion on the ML?

I hunted down the K4 Prgrammers Reference:  https://ftp.elecraft.com/K4/Manuals%20Downloads/K4%20Programmer's%20Reference,%20rev.%20D4.pdf

Two ID modes are defined:

> ID (Radio Identification)
SET/RESP format in K41 mode: IDs; where string s is "0" (default) or the user's ID text
from the status display (typically a call sign). If the string is changed via an ID command, it
will appear in the radio's status/ID area after a reboot of the radio.
RESP format in K40 mode: ID017; (GET only; for K3 compatibility).

However, as of Hamlib 4.6.0, code was added to specifically set the K4 to K40 when requesting the ID.  The fact that in K41 mode the radio can return `0` or an arbitrary string may have been deemed problematic and so the decision was to only verify that a radio of likely a K4 is at the other end of the line, seems to have been the choice.  I suspect only real reason to query the ID string in K41 mode would be to get or set the user ID string that is shown at power up (assuming it is similar to the K3 in that regard).  If so, it may be possible to do this through another Hamlib set of calls instead of the ID.

"However, as of Hamlib 4.6.0, code was added to specifically set the K4 to K40 when requesting the ID. ":

One should not arbitrarily set the K4 meta command. What should be done is to first query the radio to see what mode it is in.  Then get the ID.

This behavior is apparently expected on the part of `aclocal`.  From the Autoconf info manual documenting `aclocal`:

```
Another one is that serial numbers (*note Serials::) can be used to
update the macros in your source tree automatically when new system-wide
versions are installed.  A serial number should be a single line of the
form

     #serial NNN

where NNN contains only digits and dots.  It should appear in the M4
file before any macro definition.  It is a good practice to maintain a
serial number for each macro you distribute, even if you do not use the
‘--install’ option of ‘aclocal’: this allows other people to use it.
```

The section on serial numbers is long.  Here is the summary of their importance:

```
   Normally these serial numbers are completely ignored by ‘aclocal’ and
‘autoconf’, like any genuine comment.  However when using ‘aclocal’’s
‘--install’ feature, these serial numbers will modify the way ‘aclocal’
selects the macros to install in the package: if two files with the same
basename exist in your search path, and if at least one of them uses a
‘#serial’ line, ‘aclocal’ will ignore the file that has the older
‘#serial’ line (or the file that has none).

   Note that a serial number applies to a whole M4 file, not to any
macro it contains.  A file can contain multiple macros, but only one
serial.
```

Unfortunately, I don't find an `aclocal` option to disable this behavior.

-1 for making the token value public.

1. The tokens are found and verified based on the rig.  The compiler can't do that, so there still needs to be a lookup.  And this behooves the app to do the lookup at initialization time and stash the token if found, or perform its recovery/backup plan then instead of during operation.
2. There's no reason the token can't be different depending on the rig(for the same parameter name.)
3. In general, a "token" that is provided by a library should have no intrinsic value to the caller other than passing it back to the same library.  It should come only from calling that library, and be totally opaque to the caller.

TIL uint64_t is handled differently on CISC (e.g., x86_64) and RISC (mac M1) systems. CISC requires the %lu format while RISC requires %llu. Think that `rmode_t` and `settings_t` are already typedef'd to `uint64_t`. Think it's more about how these architectures define what that is.

Looking deeper, I think what might be complicating (perhaps even driving) the issue, is how `CONSTANT_64BIT_FLAG(BIT)` is conditionally defined. Without `SWIGLUA`, it's defined as `1ull << (BIT)`, otherwise it's `1ul << (BIT)`. Since both `rmode_t` and `settings_t` use data defined as `CONSTANT_64BIT_FLAG(BIT)` this may factor in confusing the compilers in these two architectures.

              Permits multiple AF_INET or AF_INET6 sockets to be bound to
              an identical socket address.  This option must be set on
              each socket (including the first socket) prior to calling
              [bind(2)](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/bind.2.html) on the socket.  To prevent port hijacking, all of
              the processes binding to the same address must have the
              same effective UID.  This option can be employed with both
              TCP and UDP sockets.

              For TCP sockets, this option allows [accept(2)](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/accept.2.html) load
              distribution in a multi-threaded server to be improved by
              using a distinct listener socket for each thread.  This
              provides improved load distribution as compared to
              traditional techniques such using a single [accept(2)](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/accept.2.html)ing
              thread that distributes connections, or having multiple
              threads that compete to [accept(2)](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/accept.2.html) from the same socket.

              For UDP sockets, the use of this option can provide better
              distribution of incoming datagrams to multiple processes
              (or threads) as compared to the traditional technique of
              having multiple processes compete to receive datagrams on
              the same socket.
```
