Staring at `#define RIG_ANT_MAX 32`, it seems to me to be equivalent to `RIG_ANT_6 RIG_ANT_N(5)` as 32 decimal is `00100000` in [16 bit] binary.  Perhaps the intent was to set bit 32, but that exceeds a 32 bit integer's storage space!  It's one of those things that at first glance seems reasonable and upon further thought becomes questionable.

This also brings up another question that I raised on the list some years ago, that being the use of the `_t` suffix for our defined types.  I know that is convention, but I recall reading that the C standard declares the `_t` suffix to be a reserved name space for the C library and that its use outside of the C library is discouraged.  This has made me wonder if we should adopt our own suffix such as `_hl` (not clear that it is a defined type), `_th` (more clear that it is a type, maybe), or `_thl` (probably too long!).

Most of our defined types are fairly unique and unlikely to conflict with the C library, however something like `ant_t` seems ripe for a name clash at some point.  A defined type such as `rig_ant_t` is much less likely to clash and `ant_th` would probably never clash with anything outside of Hamlib.

After all that, I think that changing the names of defined types cannot be done in Hamlib 5, it would likely have to wait until Hamlib 6, which could be five to ten years distant, if the API of Hamlib 5 is cleaned up sufficiently.  I wonder if the following would be possible, using `ant_t` as an example:

``` c
typedef unsigned int ant_t;
typedef ant_t ant_th;
```

Then, tag `ant_t` with `HL_DEPRECATED` so that a compiler warning is issued so that downstreams will be encouraged to switch to the new defined type.  Finally, Hamlib 6 would remove the `_t` defined types.  I'm sure @GeoBaltz can weigh in on whether this idea would work.

This is a possible roadmap:
* for 4.7
  * deprecations already added by George
  * possibly some more (I guess mostly pointers, not datatypes)
  * I would not delete stuff that was deprecated in 4.6 or before (because it could make life easier if the whole 4.x series is more compatible)
* for 5.0
  * delete what was deprecated in 4.7 and earlier
  * add new deprecations (mostly datatypes, eg. typedefs, enums)
* for 6.0
  * delete everything that was deprecated in previous versions

- #define -> enum - I don't see much upside to this - constants are constants, and unless they really are enumerations of distinct properties there's not much gain.
- typedef names - I think the _t suffix is only a convention, and our names are mostly unique. It does make reading the code easier. The one we should fix is the mode_t/rmode_t confusion - it may still be in some of the simulators/utilities.
- Name conflicts - definitely needs work. I made a few possibilities static, but I know at least one real one - CQRLOG has a spaces() that overrides ours.  And I'm surprised we haven't had problems with applications defining push/pop/peek.
Regarding the `_t` name space, I was merely considering the [GNU C Library rules](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Reserved-Names.html).

It was the goal of this PR to fail the configuration step if you run `./configure --with-indi --with-cxx-binding` (which is the default) and the prerequisites aren't met.

Why "yes" should be ignored?

We can change the default to `detect` or `auto` or some other word that we decide (it's just a string that must be checked to be different from "yes" and "no"):
* `detect` is the same as when no arguments are passed (the behavior is like before, ie build if the prerequisites are met, print a warning otherwise)
* `no` do not build (the behavior is like before)
* `yes` build if prerequisites are met, fail otherwise (the new behavior)

> It was the goal of this PR to fail the configuration step if you run `./configure --with-indi --with-cxx-binding` (which is the default) and the prerequisites aren't met.

That is reasonable.  Here failure should occur if the user is specifically telling `configure` to use INDI and C++ but doesn't have them installed.

> Why "yes" should be ignored?

Not at all.  It needs to be honored but in the scenario above, the user needs to be informed that optional packages requested are not available so his system needs to be fixed.  Hard failure here is perfectly acceptable.

> We can change the default to `detect` or `auto` or some other word that we decide (it's just a string that must be checked to be different from "yes" and "no"):
> 
> * `detect` is the same as when no arguments are passed (the behavior is like before, ie build if the prerequisites are met, print a warning otherwise)
> * `no` do not build (the behavior is like before)
> * `yes` build if prerequisites are met, fail otherwise (the new behavior)

I think that `detect` is the proper way to go when the command line options are not given.  When C++ is present, build those bindings and when INDI is present build its support.

If C++ is not present (rare but conceivable) then the INDI check should be bypassed.  This should probably be the case if the user passes `--without-c++-binding` to `configure`.  In both cases testing for INDI should be silently ignored and `cf_with_indi_support` set to `no`.

I hope I'm making sense!

I think the issue here is that the Makefile rule just checks the result from `diff -qN` to see if it is non-zero, whereas the actual return code from diff has different meanings (i.e. 1 means the files are different, 2 means one or more of the files does not exist).

The FreeBSD man page for diff states:

> EXIT STATUS
>      The diff utility exits with one of the following values:
> 
>            0       No differences were found.
>            1       Differences were found.
>            >1      An error occurred.

It seems that the Makefile rule should be checking for all possible cases rather than only the "no differences" case.

I was wrong about the double dollar sign: it is needed to pass `$?` tho the shell.
The rule is testing for "not zero" and it executes the part after the `||`:
> test $$? -eq 0 ||

I think we can save ourselves a lot of headaches by simplifying the approach to things.

From the Autotools perspective, FreeBSD puts additional packages in `/usr/local/[include|lib]` but it only searches `/usr/[include|lib]` which is the default GNU hierarchy for GNU system packages.  As a side note, if a newer `readline` were locally compiled on Debian and installed under `/usr/local/[include|lib]` (the default location for locally compiled packages on GNU systems), the same invocation would be required.

The easiest way for all concerned is to specify `CPPFLAGS` and `LDFLAGS` to configure as:

``` console
CPPFLAGS="-I/usr/local/include" LDFLAGS="-L/usr/local/lib" ./configure
```

In my FreeBSD VM this finds the GNU `readline` headers and libraries and compiles cleanly.  I tested with `rigctl` and there is command history.

Attached is the end portion of a run of k3test with the debug level set to TRACE. The entire file is about 1MB, and it's not very interesting. But the end portion, which basically is the part after k3test has spotted a problem, is quite revealing.

The first thing I noticed is that hamlib appears to send FA00028200000; (near the top of the attached file) which *should* cause the rig to move to that frequency, but hamlib appears to simply assume that sending that string is sufficient to guarantee success -- which of course it is not, for any number of reasons. After sending the string, there doesn't appear to be any kind of checking that the rig actually changed frequency; hamlib simply returns from the function with a RIG_OK (at least, that's my reading of the trace output).

So this would probably explain why my non-hamlib drlog functions seem to work OK whereas hamlib appears occasionally to fail: when I bypass hamlib in drlog, what I do instead is to actually check that the command had the expected effect. Elecraft actually explicitly mentions this in their otherwise-pretty-mediocre "Programmer's Reference Manual":  "A SET can be followed by a GET to verify the new settings" (page 3). 

If I read the file correctly, it also confirms that for a period of one second following a rig_set_freq(), rig_get_freq() simply returns the value that was transmitted in the most recent rig_set_freq(), without actually requesting any information from the rig at all.

I have no experience with computer control of other rigs, just my K3 and K3S. Perhaps other rigs are more reliable in actually performing the functions, although I have to say that it seems pretty dangerous to me to assume that *any* command on a remote device has been correctly executed, and to therefore omit checking. I can definitely state, though, that the K3/K3S is not particularly reliable in this regard. (In fact, one can just sit there doing nothing but sending once-per-second "IF;" commands to get the 38-byte status, and every now and then the response from the rig, even if it's the right length -- which it sometimes isn't -- contains incorrect values in some of the fields. It's rare enough that I've never bothered to try to characterise that behaviour or program around it, but it does suggest that the programming in the K3 isn't the most robust imaginable.)

Anyway, I would definitely suggest that, at least in the case of the K3, anything that is supposed to change the state of the rig in any important manner should be explicitly checked to confirm that the expected change has indeed occurred.

@dforsi  you're on the right track! I found the problem. The USB CDC driver passes data to the Pico only is DTR is set. By default, DTR is 0 in rotctl, so the solution is to call 
```
rotctl -m 602 -r /dev/ttyACM0 -vvvvvv --set-conf=dtr_state=ON
```

So here's some new info: if I leave the P3 in line, but power it down, then, so far, I have been unable to reproduce the problem. I wish I had an RS232 inline analyzer I could put between the P3 and the K3, but I don't. Absent such a device, all I can do is indulge in quasi-informed speculation.

Just to be clear, this is definitely reproducible here. P3 powered on => the reported problem exists; P3 powered off => either the problem is completely eliminated, or the probability of its occurrence is reduced to the point that it has so far been undetectable.

What I speculate, on the basis of these observations, is that there are problems in hamlib, and also in the firmware in the K3 (and perhaps the P3).

The problem in hamlib is, basically, that when it throws a command at a rig, it just seems to assume that everything is hunkydory and the rig will do what it's been told. This seems to me to be far too optimistic... who's to say that the rig: (a) receives the command exactly as it was sent; and (b) correctly acts on the command? Given that the rig control protocol contains no error detection or checking, nor any kind of delivery guarantee, nor, at least in the case of Elecraft, that a received command is absolutely guaranteed to execute, it seems to me that any command sent to the rig and intended to change the rig's state should be checked that it was actually executed. (Even in the absence of the problem we're tailing about here, a lot of shacks have enough RFI to make the assumption that serial lines work 100% correctly pretty iffy.)  And it is even more over-optimistic to cache what it expects to have have happened and return the cached state for a period of time (i.e., one second in this case) before actually checking the state.

The problems in the firmware ... well, those are harder to guess at, but the difference in behaviour between P3-powered-on and P3-powered-off suggest that whatever protection exists in the K3 to ensure that received commands aren't garbled or intermingled is not robust: it looks likely that whatever communication occurs between the P3 and the K3 (as opposed to the computer and the K3, running on the same serial line) are not always properly protected from commingling.  The protocol used by Elecraft was (obviously) designed for non-multiplexed serial lines, in a period when baud rates were low. Why they continued to use it post-(say)2000, when much more robust systems were available, I have no idea. Anyway, this is all rather irrelevant (and might be wrong anyway).

Elecraft doesn't seem to have documented the serial messaging taking place between the P3 and the K3 (at least, I can't find any documentation) but I imagine that the details depend on precisely how the P3 is set up. It may well be that you and I have our P3s configured differently, and that is why you did not see the reported issue (obviously, I'm guessing again; it's the only explanation that came to my mind -- there has to be *something* different about our setups).

# Hamlib Test Framework early design documentation

## Overview

`hamlib-test` is test framework for automated testing of Hamlib daemon implementations (rigctld, rotctld, ampctld) using declarative YAML test specifications. The framework supports both simulator mode (no hardware required) and testing on real devices.

The framework is designed to be used by Hamlib developers for automated integration testing and for backend developers to test the backend protocol implementations. It is not intended to be used by end-users to test their own devices.

The framework consists of a command-line tool that has a codebase that is separate from the Hamlib codebase and tests Hamlib through the Hamlib daemon TCP interfaces. By design, it does not link to the Hamlib library directly or use any Hamlib code.

See the end of this design document for examples of the YAML test specification format.

## Language & Build System

- **Language**: C++17
- **Build System**: CMake 3.15+
- **Platform**: Linux (primary), macOS (secondary), Windows (planned, but serial port simulation may be difficult to implement)
- **Executables**:
  - `hamlib-test` - Main CLI tool for testing Hamlib with YAML specifications
  - `hamlib-test-unit` - Unit/integration tests for the framework itself

## Dependencies

**Libraries:**
- `yaml-cpp` - YAML specification parsing and generation
- `spdlog` - Logging (console / files)
- `nlohmann_json` - Schema validation for YAML (using JSON schema) - TBD if needed

**Bundled (single-header):**
- `CLI11` - Command-line argument parsing
- `Catch2 v3` - Unit testing framework

## Main Commands

### hamlib-test run - Execute tests from a specification

Executes tests defined in a YAML specification (spec) file against Hamlib daemons. The command can operate in two distinct modes: simulator mode (default) and device mode.

In **simulator mode**, the framework acts as a virtual device (rig, rotator, amplifier). Depending on the device communication method, the framework creates a pseudo-terminal (PTY) or TCP server that presents itself to the Hamlib daemon as if it were real hardware. When the daemon sends protocol commands, the simulator validates them against expected sequences defined in the specification and responds accordingly. This mode requires no physical hardware and provides fast, reproducible testing of the  Hamlib backend protocol implementations.

In **device mode**, the framework connects the Hamlib daemon to real hardware via serial port or network connection. Tests execute Hamlib commands and validate only the Hamlib daemon responses without inspecting the underlying protocol traffic. This mode validates that real devices behave as expected.

```bash
# Simulator mode (no hardware)
hamlib-test run -f specification.yaml

# Device mode (real hardware)
hamlib-test run -f specification.yaml --mode device --port /dev/ttyUSB0

# Filter by tags
hamlib-test run -f specification.yaml --tags smoke,basic
```

### hamlib-test generate - Generate a specification using Hamlib device capabilities

The `generate` command generates a YAML specification file by querying Hamlib device capabilities and generating appropriate test commands. The specification can then be used as a starting point for creating a full set of test cases and for inspecting the particular Hamlib device backend protocol implementation.

The process begins by spawning the appropriate Hamlib daemon with the `--dump-caps` flag to retrieve all capabilities for the specified model. The framework parses the capabilities to understand what features the device supports.

Based on these capabilities, the framework generates a comprehensive set of test commands covering all supported functionality. For rigs, this includes commands spanning frequency control, mode selection, VFO operations, PTT, levels, functions, and parameters. For rotators, commands for position and movement are generated. For amplifiers, commands covering frequency, levels, and power control are created.

The framework then executes the generated commands against a running Hamlib daemon while a **proxy transport** (two pseudo-terminals for serial port communication or a TCP server and client for network communication) records all protocol traffic exchanged between the daemon and the real device. Finally, the framework converts the recorded traffic into YAML test sequences.

```bash
# Generate complete specification
hamlib-test generate --model 3073 -o ic7300.yaml

# Generate specific categories only
hamlib-test generate --model 3073 --categories frequency,mode -o basic.yaml
```

### hamlib-test validate - Validate a specification file against the schema

Validates a YAML specification file against the framework's JSON schema and performs semantic checks. The validation ensures that all required fields are present, data types are correct, protocol handler names are valid and available, and the overall structure conforms to the specification format specification.

Validation errors include line numbers and helpful suggestions for common mistakes, making it easier to author and debug specifications.

```bash
# Validate specification
hamlib-test validate -f specification.yaml
```

## How the Commands Work

### Simulator Mode Testing

When running tests in simulator mode, the framework loads the YAML specification and parses it into internal data structures, validating the schema and ensuring all required components are present. It then creates the appropriate protocol handler based on the specification's protocol specification (such as Icom CI-V, Kenwood CAT, or Yaesu NEWCAT).

The framework establishes the necessary transport mechanisms, which may include creating pseudo-terminals for serial communication or TCP servers for network-based protocols. Multiple transports can be created simultaneously to support devices that use separate connections for CAT commands, I/Q or audio streaming, and other functions.

Command/response pairs defined in the specification `commands` section are loaded into the device simulator. These pairs define how the simulator should respond to protocol commands during different phases (initialization, testing, and teardown).

The framework spawns the appropriate Hamlib daemon (rigctld, rotctld, or ampctld) configured to communicate with the simulator transport endpoints.

For each test case, the framework sends the specified Hamlib command to the daemon. Concurrently, the simulator monitors the protocol transport for incoming commands. When protocol commands arrive, the simulator validates them against the expected sequence defined in the test `seq` section and sends the appropriate responses. The framework then captures the Hamlib daemon response and validates it against the expected results of the test case, recording success or failure along with detailed timing and error information.

### Device Mode Testing

Device mode follows a simpler flow since no simulation is required. The framework spawns the Hamlib daemon configured to communicate directly with real hardware via the specified serial port or network address. Tests execute by sending Hamlib commands and validating only the Hamlib daemon responses without inspecting the underlying protocol traffic. This approach verifies that the real device behaves as expected and that the test specification is valid for the device.

### Specification Generation

The specification generation process begins by executing the Hamlib daemon capability dump command to retrieve comprehensive information about what the device supports. This text output is parsed into structured capability data including frequency ranges, operating modes, VFO configurations, available functions, and settable levels, etc.

Using these capabilities, the framework generates test commands automatically. For example, if a rig supports USB and LSB modes across multiple frequency ranges, the generator creates appropriate set_mode and set_frequency commands using realistic values. The generator respects device limitations, only creating commands for features the device actually supports.

These generated commands are executed against a running Hamlib daemon while a proxy transport sits between the daemon and a simulated device. The proxy records all protocol traffic, capturing the exact byte sequences exchanged during each command execution. Response parsing extracts the Hamlib daemon responses and determines expected values.

Finally, all recorded data is assembled into a complete YAML specification structure with metadata, protocol configuration, command/response pairs, and test cases including protocol sequences. This specification can then be used for regression testing or further refined manually.

## Protocol Handlers

The framework includes built-in support for major amateur radio protocols through the use of protocol handlers.

The **Icom CI-V** protocol handler manages Icom's binary protocol, automatically adding frame wrappers (FE FE preamble, destination/source addresses, and FD terminator) around command payloads. Specifications specify only the payload bytes while the handler manages framing.

The **Kenwood CAT** protocol handler processes Kenwood's text-based command protocol, which uses semicolon terminators. Commands are ASCII text strings that the handler validates and terminates appropriately.

The **Yaesu NEWCAT** protocol handler supports Yaesu's newer text-based protocol, similar to Kenwood but with protocol-specific command structures and responses.

**Raw text** and **raw binary** protocol handlers provide pass-through functionality for protocols not yet specifically implemented, allowing the framework to work with any device by treating protocol data as opaque byte sequences.

## YAML Specification Format

Specifications are declarative YAML files that define device metadata, protocol configuration, command/response pairs for simulation, and test cases with expected results.

The **meta** section identifies the device type (rig, rotator, or amplifier), Hamlib model ID, manufacturer, and model name. The **protocol** section specifies which protocol handler to use, handler-specific configuration (such as CI-V addresses or command terminators), and transport definitions for serial ports, TCP connections, or UDP endpoints.

The **commands** section defines how the simulator responds during different phases. Each command/response pair specifies a matching pattern (exact, prefix, or regex), the response to send, which phases it's available in (init, test, teardown), and a description. This allows the simulator to respond differently during daemon initialization versus actual testing.

The **tests** section contains individual test cases. Each test specifies a unique identifier, the Hamlib command to execute (like `f` for get frequency or `F` for set frequency with arguments), the expected protocol sequence (transmit and receive steps showing exactly what protocol bytes should be exchanged), and the expected Hamlib response status and values.

Protocol sequences use `tx` steps to represent commands the simulator receives from the daemon (and validates) and `rx` steps for responses the simulator sends back. Protocol data is represented as hex strings for binary protocols like CI-V (e.g., "03 00 74 04 14 00") or text strings for text-based protocols like Kenwood (e.g., "FA00014074000").

## Current Status

The framework is currently in the early stages of development with a private ("throw-away") proof-of-concept codebase implementation that is able to run simple tests for the Icom CI-V, Kenwood CAT, and Yaesu NEWCAT protocols using both the simulator mode and device mode.

The next step (milestone 2 in the project plan) is to clean up the codebase for publication and to make the framework functional for full testing of at least two rigs: Icom IC-7610 and Kenwood TS-480 - to represent two commonly used CAT protocols. After this, the framework code will be open for public review and contribution. As the this ARDC Hamlib improvement project progresses, the framework will be updated to support new rigs, protocols and features.

## Example YAML test specifications

* [ts480_minimal.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23699154/ts480_minimal.yaml) - A test specification example for TS-480 (Kenwood protocol)
* [ic7300_minimal.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23699160/ic7300_minimal.yaml) - A test specification example for IC-7300 (Icom CI-V protocol)

Minimal specification generation example for TS-480: [ts480_generated.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23699176/ts480_generated.yaml)

```yaml
# Kenwood TS-480 minimal test specification example for unit testing of the Kenwood CAT protocol handler

meta:
  device: rig
  model_id: 2028
  model: TS-480
  manufacturer: Kenwood
  format: "1.0"
  description: "Minimal TS-480 test specification example for unit testing of the Kenwood CAT protocol handler"

protocol:
  handler: kenwood
  config:
    terminator: ";"
  transports:
    # In addition to serial transport, also TCP (client) transport will be supported and there are plans to see how UDP transport would work with UDP protocols, such as the Icom network protocol.
    - name: cat
      type: serial
      config:
        baudrate: "115200"
        data_bits: "8"
        stop_bits: "2"
        parity: "none"
        flow_control: "none"

# Specification-wide setup - executed once before all tests
setup:
  commands:
    - command:
        value: "ID"
      match_response:
        type: exact
        value: "ID020"
      description: "Read radio ID during setup"
    - command:
        value: "FA00014074000"
      match_response:
        # There are three match types supported for match_response: none,exact, prefix, and regex
        # none: no response validation
        # exact: match the exact response
        # prefix: match the response prefix (e.g. "FA" will match "FA00014074000", but not "FA")
        # regex: match the response regex (e.g. "MD([1-9])" will match "MD2", but not "MD10")
        type: none
      description: "Set VFO A to 14.074 MHz (no response validation)"

# Specification-wide teardown - executed once after all tests
teardown:
  commands:
    - command:
        value: "FR"
      match_response:
        type: exact
        value: "FR0"
      description: "Read active RX VFO during teardown - expect VFO A"

# Command/response pairs for device simulation
# The device simulator will accept and response to the specified commands during the specified phases (setup, test, teardown).
# Note: All values are ASCII strings representing CAT payload without terminator
commands:
  # Setup phase - Radio identification and power-up sequence

  - match_command:
      # There are three match types supported for match_command: exact, prefix, and regex
      # exact: match the exact command
      # prefix: match the command prefix (e.g. "FA" will match "FA00014074000", but not "FA")
      # regex: match the command regex (e.g. "MD([1-9])" will match "MD2", but not "MD10")
      type: exact
      value: "ID"
    response:
      value: "ID020"
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Request radio ID (TS-480 = 020) - first command in kenwood_open()"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "TY"
    response:
      value: "TY001"
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Request rig type/model info (TS-480SAT = 1) - used by rigctl_get_info() (info command '_')"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "PS"
    response:
      value: "PS1"
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Query power status - returns ON (1)"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "PS1"
    response:
      value: "PS1"
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Set power ON - sent if auto_power_on enabled"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "FA"
    response:
      value: "FA00014074000"
    phases: [setup, test, teardown]
    description: "Query VFO A frequency - fallback verification (14.074 MHz)"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "AI"
    response:
      value: "AI0"
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Query auto-info mode status"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "AI0"
    response:
      # For commands with no response, the response value is an empty string
      value: ""
    phases: [setup]
    description: "Disable auto-info mode"

  # Test phase - commands accepted from Hamlib during test execution, in addition to the actual test sequences (allows flexibility for the test framework)

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "IF"
    response:
      value: "IF00014074000     +000000000200000000"
    phases: [setup, test]
    description: "Get transceiver information (freq, mode, VFO, etc.)"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "KS"
    response:
      value: "KS025"
    phases: [setup, test]
    description: "Query CW keyer speed - default 25 WPM"

  # Test phase - Mode and filter operations

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "MD"
    response:
      value: "MD2"
    phases: [test]
    description: "Query current mode - USB (2)"

  - match_command:
      type: prefix
      value: "MD"
    response:
      value: "MD{0}"
    phases: [test]
    description: "Set mode - echo back the mode code"

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "FW"
    response:
      value: "FW0000"
    phases: [test]
    description: "Query filter width - returns narrow filter"

  # Teardown phase - commands accepted from Hamlib after all tests have completed

  - match_command:
      type: exact
      value: "PS0"
    response:
      value: ""
    phases: [teardown]
    description: "Power off radio"

# Test cases
tests:
  - id: get_freq_basic
    name: Get frequency - VFO A
    description: Read current frequency from VFO A
    tags: [basic, frequency, smoke]
    # Individual test cases may have setup and teardown commands that are not part of the specification-wide setup and teardown
    setup:
      commands:
        - command:
            value: "FR0"
          match_response:
            type: none
          description: "Set receive VFO to VFO A during setup"
        - command:
            value: "FA00014074000"
          match_response:
            type: none
          description: "Set VFO A frequency to 14.074 MHz during setup"
    teardown:
      commands:
        - command:
            value: "FR0"
          match_response:
            type: none
          description: "Set receive VFO to VFO A during teardown"
    cmd:
      op: f
    seq:
      - tx:
          data:
            raw: "FA"
      - rx:
          data:
            raw: "FA00014074000"
    expect:
      status: RIG_OK
      # Match Hamlib extended response format values
      values:
        "Frequency": "14074000"

  - id: set_freq_basic
    name: Set frequency - VFO A
    description: Set VFO A frequency to 7.040 MHz

    cmd:
      op: F

    seq:
      - tx:
          data:
            raw: "FA"
      - rx:
          data:
            raw: "FA00014074000"
      - tx:
          data:
            raw: "FA00007040000"
      - tx:
          data:
            raw: "ID"
      - rx:
          data:
            raw: "ID019"
    expect:
      status: RIG_OK
```

@N0NB @dforsi @GeoBaltz Do we really need the dump_state anywhere? The dump_state format is difficult for clients to parse correctly and it's also specific to internal Hamlib data structures - which should be allowed to change.

Why am I raising this here -> I will need to adapt dump_caps format to new features we introduce next year as a part of the ARDC project (https://github.com/orgs/Hamlib/projects/1), so instead of extending the difficult-to-parse textual dump_caps format forever, I'd go for properly structured JSON output. After all, JSON is already used in Hamlib in certain places and there's a built-in library for it.

In 5.0, I'd suggest we'd start a transition to machine parseable JSON interface:
 
- Remove dump_state (deprecate it in next 4.x release?)
- Make sure dump_caps has all dump_state information
- Freeze dump_caps output at 5.0 - so it will not get new updates and will force future clients to use JSON format instead.
- Add a JSON version of dump_caps output and add any changes 
- Maybe even adapt JSON in all commands and responses -> we'd keep the current response formats (short + extended), but add a new "JSON" format, which would be opt-in.

For example, now `+\get_freq` gives you the extended response like:
```
Frequency: 145000000
```

Instead, we could even go as far as having commands in JSON format for very easy parsing, e.g.
```
{"command": "get_freq"}
```

Response:
```
{"Frequency":145000000}
```

The parser could easily detect JSON commands by checking the first character of the command, e.g. `{` for JSON and `+` for extended response, `\` for long format commands or one of the single char commands.

This allows clients to migrate to JSON format command-by-command (e.g. only use JSON for dump_caps for a start), making gradual migration possible.

My guess is that "dump_state" is more of a debugging tool than anything useful by a client app, though I could be completely wrong on that.

Welcome to Open Source projects!  It's always a good thing when people want to participate and improve a project.  There's no hard and fast 'rule' to open source contribution in general, though individual projects may have their own specal requirements or practices.  That being said, for a large project like this, it is generally best practice to follow conventions from the existing project, and try to keep the code similar, so that there aren't super varied sections that become difficumt for others to read understand or maintain.  In the case of the monolithic file, since that's how all of the other radios work, it just makes sense to keep with that strategy so that someone coming along can have consistency in how it's done.  If you wanted to propose a refactor to ALL of the code to break it up into many files, and work on that, that's something that could be possible, but everyone's going to have their own opinion, so defaulting to how it already is unless there's a signifigant reason to change it (outside of personal preference) is likely the standard path.  This goes for the test file stuff as well.  It's interesting and useful perhaps for other developers if they intend to make modifications, but as not every radio has these types of files, and there's not a standard suite for the tests as part of the project, it might be cluttered and confusing to anyone viewing this secrion of the code.  When developing the existing code I also had several similar test files, but didn't think they needed to be part of the actual codebase.  Also if there's existing (working!) code, simply ripping that out and replacing it entirely (and removing previous contributer credits in the process) is possibly not an ideal path.  Would it be possible to instead modify the existing code to add any functions that were missing, or to correct any that are not functioning?  It took a bt of a mental change for myself as well when i first started working on collaborative projects, but when a project is being worked on by several people, it's often best to modify things that are existing already, and do it im small incremental batches, so that things can be more easily understood and worked on as a team.  This was also what motivated me to take the existing 991A code as my basis for starting the FTX-1 work, so that there was consistency, and then to come back and make changes (for example there's definitely still some simple stuff that's blatantly wrong in the code like saying there is no antenna selection)

Anyhow I really hope this isn't in any way coming across as discouraging, as I want to simply present the view that I have of contributing to projects like this.  This isn't -MY- project so nothing I say is particularly more important than anything anyone else says, but seeing the entirety of the code I wrote ripped out was surprising, so I figured I'd pop in and lend some perspective.
No offense at all!  Welcome to the project.  I commented more in your PR, but definitely look foward to working together and whatever direction we can get the code going for other users.

Done. Spent all day yesterday testing the Field configuration and all day to day testing the Optima configuration. I'm still finding a few corner cases in some extended commands, but core Hamlib should be pretty solid.

**FTX-1 split handling problem with satellite tracking software (GPredict etc.)**

The Yaesu FTX-1 has two independent VFOs (MAIN and SUB), but its behavior in Split mode is fundamentally different from typical satellite-capable transceivers.

Through extensive testing with Hamlib and GPredict by myself, the following behavior has been confirmed:

- When Hamlib receives S 1 1 (Split ON, TX VFO specified) from GPredict and forwards it to the FTX-1 backend,
- the radio immediately forces the SUB VFO into TX/PTT state (red TX lamp on),
- while in this state, the SUB VFO frequency can no longer be changed,
- as a result, it becomes impossible to control uplink and downlink frequencies independently.

In other words, FTX-1 Split mode cannot be used for satellite operation, because enabling Split on the radio itself breaks frequency control and forces unwanted PTT behavior.

However, satellite tracking software such as GPredict always sends Split commands first, and then controls RX/TX frequencies separately.
Changing this behavior on the GPredict side is not realistic, because it would affect many other rigs that rely on standard Split semantics.

Therefore, the problem must be handled inside Hamlib.

**Proposed approach**

For FTX-1 only:

- When Hamlib receives Split commands (e.g. S 1 1) from clients such as GPredict,
- Hamlib should not forward Split commands to the FTX-1 backend.
- Instead, Split state should be handled internally inside Hamlib.

Hamlib should then:

- send the downlink frequency to MAIN VFO,
- send the uplink frequency to SUB VFO, 
- internally remember which VFO is used for TX,
- and ensure that when the uplink is on SUB, the SUB VFO is used as TX without putting the radio into its native Split mode.

This effectively emulates satellite split operation inside Hamlib, while keeping the FTX-1 itself out of Split mode.

**Rationale**

- This avoids the FTX-1 firmware limitation where SUB becomes locked in TX/PTT state.
- It preserves compatibility with existing satellite tracking software.
- The workaround is strictly limited to FTX-1 and does not affect other rigs.

At present, without such handling, **it is impossible to operate the FTX-1 with GPredict for satellite Doppler correction,** despite the radio having two VFOs.

**Important FTX-1 specific detail**

The FTX-1 is fundamentally different from traditional Yaesu rigs:
- It has two fully independent receivers (MAIN and SUB), not a classic split VFO model.
- Enabling hardware split (ST1) forces SUB into TX/PTT state, which breaks satellite operation because SUB frequency can no longer be updated.
- For satellite tracking, the correct behavior is:
　- Do not enable hardware split on the radio
　- Track downlink and uplink frequencies independently on MAIN and SUB
　- Use SUB as the TX VFO logically, without asserting PTT or hardware split

- Completely suppressing the ST command for FTX-1 in Hamlib
- Handling satellite-style split entirely inside Hamlib (pure virtual split)

Hi KJ5HST,

Thank you for your work and for pointing me to your Hamlib-FTX1 fork (ftx1-backend).
After cloning your fork, building, and running make install, the original issue where Sub VFO unexpectedly goes into TX no longer occurs. So your fixes clearly address that problem 👍

However, when testing with GPredict, I am still observing an issue where **Uplink and Downlink frequencies are shown as the same value on the GPredict side**. After analyzing the rigctld -vvvvv log in detail, I believe the cause is now clearer, so I’d like to summarize it technically.

**Summary of the observed behavior**

GPredict appears to be misled by the sequence and semantics of Hamlib responses in split mode, specifically the interaction between:

- f (get_freq)
- i (get_split_freq)
- internal caching of currVFO when split=1

As a result, GPredict ends up treating the **TX (uplink) frequency as if it were the RX (downlink) frequency**.

**Evidence from the rigctld debug log**

1. Split mode is enabled correctly

> rigctl: S 1 Main
> Split: 1
> TX VFO: Main


2. RX frequency is set and read correctly at first

> F 435612000
> f -> 435612000


3.TX (uplink) frequency is set via split

> I 145993000
> FB145993000;


4.Hamlib correctly reports TX frequency

> i -> 145993000


5.Problematic behavior
  Shortly after this, GPredict issues:

> f


  and Hamlib responds with:

> rig_get_freq: Main cache hit
> freq=145993000


  At this point, f (which GPredict interprets as downlink / RX frequency) returns the TX frequency instead.

**Technical interpretation**

From the log, it looks like:

- In split mode (split=1), currVFO remains Main
- After rig_set_split_freq() updates the TX frequency, the Main VFO cache is updated
- Subsequent rig_get_freq(currVFO) calls return the TX frequency, not the RX frequency
- GPredict assumes:
  - f → Downlink
  - i → Uplink
     which is consistent with Hamlib’s public API expectations

So while the backend behavior is internally consistent, the Hamlib-level semantics no longer match what GPredict expects, leading GPredict to display identical uplink/downlink frequencies.

**Why this matters for GPredict**

GPredict does not explicitly manage VFO tokens.
It relies on:

- f → RX (downlink)
- i → TX (uplink)

Therefore, if f ever returns the TX frequency in split mode, GPredict cannot distinguish them and will always show both as the same value.

**Current status on my side**

- ✅ Sub VFO TX issue is fixed using your fork
- ❌ GPredict still shows identical uplink/downlink frequencies
- Root cause appears to be frequency cache / currVFO handling in split mode, not GPredict itself

I’ve attached the full rigctld -vvvvv log so the exact sequence can be reviewed.

Thanks again for your work — the backend is very close now, and I hope this analysis helps pinpoint the remaining issue.

I can confirm this. We encountered the same root cause while working on the FTX-1 code (PR #1961) when someone reported that GPredict didn't work with the radio in split. In addition to finding out that the radio has a firmware bug to work around, we also discovered that there is cache corruption between VFOA/MAIN slots during split. The Hamlib core's optimization is problematic because it trusts stale cache data. 

We worked around it by:
  - Always sending the command (never skipping)
  - Explicitly managing cache for both VFOs
  - Using private state to track and restore correct values

---
Specifically, here's how we fixed it:

1. We bypass the core's optimization - ftx1_set_split_freq() sends `FB<freq>;` directly to the radio every time. We don't rely on the core's "skip if same" logic.
2. Proactive cache management - Lines 470-499 in ftx1_vfo.c:
```
  saved_main_freq = cachep->freqMainA;  // Save before corruption
  // ... send command to radio ...
  rig_set_cache_freq(rig, RIG_VFO_SUB, tx_freq);  // Cache for SUB explicitly
  priv->ftx1_cache_fix_freq = saved_main_freq;    // Save for restoration
  priv->ftx1_cache_fix_needed = 1;
```
3. Cache restoration - In ftx1_get_split_freq() we restore the Main cache before it's read:
```
  if (priv->ftx1_cache_fix_needed)
  {
      cachep->freqMainA = priv->ftx1_cache_fix_freq;
      priv->ftx1_cache_fix_needed = 0;
  }
```
4. Force correct VFO - We always set 'tx_vfo = RIG_VFO_SUB' when split is ON, avoiding VFOA/MAIN cache slot aliasing. This also follows the Yaesu CAT documentation where SUB is always TX and MAIN is always RX when Split is enabled.

It seems that this matter (`dumpcaps()` vs `dumpstate()` functions vs the `\dump_state` command) is rather complex in Hamlib. I went through the code myself first and also let a certain "random generator" create documentation on what's going on (as a separate message).

## Status and proposed changes

Here are the details summarized: (written by me as I understand things)

* The `dumpcaps()` function is the most straightforward - it's used by the `\dump_caps` Hamlib command and outputs the _static_ capabilities defined for a device (rig/rotator/amplifier). This is essentially the data in the statically defined structs in device backend.

## PART 1: `dumpcaps()` vs `dumpstate()` Functions

### What are they?

Both are **human-readable** output functions in `tests/dumpcaps.c` (1303 lines) and `tests/dumpstate.c` (1080 lines). They produce nearly identical output with the same format (tab-separated labels, same structure).

### Key difference: Data source

| Aspect | `dumpcaps()` | `dumpstate()` |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| Reads from | `rig->caps` (static backend definition) | `rig_state` / `rs` (runtime state, copied from caps at init) |
| Includes | `dumpcaps.h`, targetable VFO feature breakdown, range_sanity_check, ts_sanity_check, dumpconf/dumpconf_list helpers, `chan->split` field | None of these extras |
| Buffer | `prntbuf[8192]` | `prntbuf[4096]` |
| `rig_type` array | non-static | `static` |

The runtime `rig_state` fields start as copies of `rig->caps` values but can be **modified at runtime** (e.g., the netrigctl backend populates `rig_state` from the remote daemon's `dump_state` response). This is the fundamental reason `dumpstate()` exists: when connected to a remote rigctld, `rig->caps` reflects the *netrigctl* backend's own caps, not the actual remote hardware. Only `rig_state` has the correct data received from the remote end.

### `dumpstate()` has LESS content

`dumpcaps()` includes these sections that `dumpstate()` lacks:
- Targetable VFO feature breakdown (FREQ, MODE, TONE, FUNC, LEVEL, etc. - 14 individual bits)
- `range_sanity_check()` and `ts_sanity_check()` validation functions
- `dumpconf()`, `dumpconf_list()`, `dumpconf_list_rot()` helper functions
- `chan->split` capability in channel dump
- Backend warning accumulation and summary

### All call sites

| Function | File | Line | Context |
|----------|------|------|---------|
| `dumpstate()` | `tests/rigctl_parse.c:4660` | In `dump_caps` command handler | Only when `rig_model == RIG_MODEL_NETRIGCTL` |
| `dumpstate()` | `tests/rigctl.c:620` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | Only when `my_model == RIG_MODEL_NETRIGCTL` |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctl_parse.c:4665` | In `dump_caps` command handler | For all non-netrigctl backends |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctl.c:625` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | For all non-netrigctl backends |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctld.c:683` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | Always |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctlcom.c:515` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | Always |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctltcp.c:646` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | Always |
| `dumpcaps()` | `tests/rigctlsync.c:534` | CLI `--dump-caps` option | Always |

**Note: There is a bug** at `tests/rigctl_parse.c:4658-4660` - the code creates a `cmd` string `"\\dump_caps\n"` but never sends it, then just calls `dumpstate()` locally. The `cmd` variable is unused.

### Can we consolidate?

**Yes, fairly easily for Hamlib 5.0.** The solution is straightforward:

1. Make `dumpcaps()` read from `rig_state` instead of `rig->caps` (same as `dumpstate()` already does)
2. Add the missing extras from `dumpcaps()` back (targetable VFO breakdown, sanity checks, etc.)
3. Delete `dumpstate()` and `tests/dumpstate.c` entirely
4. Use `dumpcaps()` everywhere, including for netrigctl

The reason `dumpstate()` was created as a separate copy was because `dumpcaps()` read from `caps` (static) while netrigctl needed `rig_state` (runtime). But now that Hamlib has been migrating fields from `caps` to `rig_state` anyway, making `dumpcaps()` read from `rig_state` is the clean solution. For non-netrigctl backends, `rig_state` values are identical to `caps` values after `rig_init()`.

**No rotator/amplifier equivalent exists** - `dumpcaps_rot()` and `dumpcaps_amp()` have no `dumpstate` counterpart, so those are already clean.

## PART 2: `dump_state` Command (wire protocol)

### What is it?

The `dump_state` command (code `0x8f`) is a **machine-readable** protocol command handled by rigctld/rotctld/ampctld. It is **completely different** from the human-readable `dumpstate()` function despite the similar name.

It's a **wire protocol** that network backends (netrigctl, netrotctl, netampctl, quisk) send to a daemon on connection to discover the remote rig's capabilities.

### Implementation locations

| Daemon | File | Lines | Protocol Version |
|--------|------|-------|-----------------|
| rigctld | `tests/rigctl_parse.c:4673-4891` | 220 lines | `RIGCTLD_PROT_VER 1` |
| rotctld | `tests/rotctl_parse.c:2448-2535` | 88 lines | `ROTCTLD_PROT_VER 1` |
| ampctld | `tests/ampctl_parse.c:2408-2443` | 36 lines | `AMPCTLD_PROT_VER 0` |

### Output format (rig, the most complex)

**Protocol v0** (positional, always output):
```
1                          # protocol version
2                          # rig model ID
0                          # ITU region (deprecated, always 0)
14000000 14350000 0x1f ... # RX ranges (terminated by "0 0 0 0 0 0 0")
14000000 14350000 0x1f ... # TX ranges (terminated by "0 0 0 0 0 0 0")
0x1f 10                    # tuning steps (terminated by "0 0")
0x1f 2400                  # filters (terminated by "0 0")
25000                      # max RIT
25000                      # max XIT
0                          # max IF shift
0                          # announces
10 20                      # preamp values (newline-terminated)
10 20                      # attenuator values (newline-terminated)
0xfff                      # has_get_func bitmask
0xfff                      # has_set_func bitmask
0xfff                      # has_get_level bitmask
0xfff                      # has_set_level bitmask
0x0                        # has_get_parm bitmask
0x0                        # has_set_parm bitmask
```

**Protocol v1** (tag=value, only emitted after `chk_vfo` command has been sent):
```
vfo_ops=0x1f
ptt_type=0x0
targetable_vfo=0x0
has_set_vfo=1
has_get_vfo=1
has_set_freq=1
has_get_freq=1
has_set_conf=0
has_get_conf=0
has_get_ant=0
has_set_ant=0
has_power2mW=0
has_mW2power=0
timeout=1000
rig_model=2
rigctld_version=Hamlib 4.6~git
agc_levels=0 1 2 3
ctcss_list= 67.0 71.9 ...
dcs_list= 23 25 ...
level_gran=0=0,0,0;1=0,0,0;...
parm_gran=0=0,0,0;...
rig_model=2
hamlib_version=Hamlib 4.6~git
done
```

### All consumers (parsers of `dump_state` output)

| Backend | File | Lines | Complexity |
|---------|------|-------|-----------|
| netrigctl | `rigs/dummy/netrigctl.c` | ~290-922 | **630+ lines** - parses full v0+v1 protocol |
| netrotctl | `rigs/dummy/netrotctl.c` | ~66-156 | ~90 lines - parses v0+v1 |
| netampctl | `rigs/dummy/netampctl.c` | ~62-119 | ~60 lines - minimal, just reads version + model |
| quisk | `rigs/dummy/quisk.c` | ~200-600 | **400+ lines** - identical logic to netrigctl |

**No external consumers found** in the repository. The `dump_state` command is purely internal to Hamlib's network backend architecture.

### What's in `dump_state` that's NOT in `dump_caps`?

The `dump_state` command output contains some data that `dump_caps` (the human-readable command '1') does **not** show or shows differently:

| Data | `dump_state` | `dump_caps` (human) |
|------|-------------|-------------------|
| Protocol version number | Yes | No |
| `has_set_vfo`, `has_get_vfo`, etc. (function pointer presence) | Yes (v1, as `=0`/`=1`) | Yes (listed as "Can get/set X: Y") |
| `level_gran` / `parm_gran` (full numeric granularity arrays) | Yes (v1, compact format) | Partially (human-readable) |
| `vfo_ops` bitmask | Yes (v1) | Yes (as text list) |
| `ptt_type` bitmask | Yes (v1) | Yes (as text description) |
| Frequency ranges as numeric tuples | Yes (v0) | Yes (formatted with MHz) |

**In practice**: `dump_state` and `dump_caps` contain the same *information*, but `dump_state` is structured for machine parsing while `dump_caps` is formatted for humans.

### Rotator `dump_state` unique data

The rotator `dump_state` includes runtime position limits (`min_az`, `max_az`, `min_el`, `max_el`) with **offset adjustments** applied (`rs->min_az + rs->az_offset`), plus `south_zero` and `rot_type`. The rotator `dump_caps` does NOT include these offset-adjusted values.

### Amplifier `dump_state` - almost empty

The amp `dump_state` is extremely minimal (protocol v0 only) - just outputs protocol version and a hardcoded model name string. Almost no useful data.

## PART 3: Migration Strategy to JSON-based `dump_caps`

### Goal: Replace `dump_state` with JSON `dump_caps`

Since we're targeting Hamlib 5.0 (breaking API changes allowed):

**Phase 1 - Unify `dumpcaps()`/`dumpstate()`:**
1. Make `dumpcaps()` read from `rig_state` instead of `rig->caps`
2. Delete `dumpstate()` and `tests/dumpstate.c`
3. Remove netrigctl special-case in `dump_caps` command handler

**Phase 2 - Add JSON output to `dump_caps`:**
1. Add a JSON output mode to `dumpcaps()` / `dumpcaps_rot()` / `dumpcaps_amp()`
2. Include ALL data currently in `dump_state` (frequency ranges, granularity, bitmasks, etc.)
3. The JSON must include everything netrigctl/netrotctl/netampctl/quisk currently parse from `dump_state`

**Phase 3 - Migrate network backends:**
1. Change netrigctl to send `\dump_caps` (requesting JSON) instead of `\dump_state`
2. Rewrite the parser in netrigctl.c (~630 lines of positional parsing -> JSON parsing)
3. Do the same for netrotctl.c, netampctl.c, quisk.c
4. **JSON library needed**: Hamlib doesn't currently use a JSON library. Options:
   - cJSON (lightweight, single-file, MIT license)
   - jansson (more full-featured)
   - Hand-rolled minimal JSON writer (for output only) + parser

**Phase 4 - Remove `dump_state`:**
1. Remove the `dump_state` command handler from rigctl_parse.c, rotctl_parse.c, ampctl_parse.c
2. Remove command entry `0x8f` from all test_list tables
3. Update man pages

### Backwards compatibility considerations (for information only)

- Old rigctld (v4) + New rigctl client (v5): Client sends `\dump_caps` with JSON request, old daemon doesn't understand -> would need fallback to `\dump_state`
- New rigctld (v5) + Old rigctl client (v4): Old client sends `\dump_state`, new daemon doesn't have it -> broken
- **For Hamlib 5.0**: Since it's a major version break, we can simply document that v5 clients require v5 daemons. No mixed-version support needed.

## PART 4: Deep Dive - `dumpcaps()` vs `dumpstate()` Field-by-Field Differences

### Why does `dumpstate()` exist?

The netrigctl backend connects to a remote rigctld daemon. When this happens:
- `rig->caps` contains the **local** netrigctl backend definition (generic/dummy capabilities)
- `rig_state` (rs) gets populated from the **remote** daemon's `dump_state` response during `netrigctl_open()`

So for netrigctl, `caps` is "wrong" (it describes the network backend, not the actual radio), while `rig_state` is "right" (it has the remote radio's actual capabilities). This is the sole reason `dumpstate()` was created as a copy of `dumpcaps()` reading from `rs` instead of `caps`.

### Field-by-field comparison

For each field, we note whether netrigctl actually populates it in `rig_state` from the remote daemon. Fields NOT populated by netrigctl will have default/zeroed values in `rig_state` for network rigs, making `dumpstate()` output **incorrect** for those fields.

#### Inconsistencies found

1. **`ctcss_list` / `dcs_list`**: netrigctl populates **caps** (lines 783-797) but NOT `rig_state`. So `dumpstate()` reading from `rs->ctcss_list` would get NULL/empty for network rigs while `dumpcaps()` reading from `caps->ctcss_list` would be correct. This is a bug in `dumpstate()`.

2. Fix netrigctl to populate `rig_state` for ctcss_list, dcs_list, timeout, level_gran, parm_gran

4. Delete `dumpstate()` entirely

| `agc_levels` | via `rig_sprintf_agc_levels(rig, ...)` | NO - static caps |
| `ctcss_list` | `rig->caps->ctcss_list` | NO - static caps |
| `dcs_list` | `rig->caps->dcs_list` | NO - static caps |
| `level_gran[]` | `rs->level_gran` | NO - copied from caps at `rig_init()` (rig.c:865,971) |
| `parm_gran[]` | `rs->parm_gran` | NO - copied from caps at `rig_init()` (rig.c:972) |
| `hamlib_version` | `hamlib_version2` | NO - build-time constant |

**Interesting observation**: The v1 section reads mostly from `rig->caps` directly, while v0 reads from `rig_state`. This is inconsistent - both are reading static data, just from different copies.

#### Rotator `dump_state` - one exception

| Field | Source | Truly dynamic? |
|-------|--------|---------------|
| `min_az + az_offset` | `rs->min_az + rs->az_offset` | **PARTIALLY** - `az_offset` is configurable via `rot_set_conf()` |
| `max_az + az_offset` | `rs->max_az + rs->az_offset` | **PARTIALLY** - same |
| `min_el + el_offset` | `rs->min_el + rs->el_offset` | **PARTIALLY** - `el_offset` is configurable |
| `max_el + el_offset` | `rs->max_el + rs->el_offset` | **PARTIALLY** - same |
| `south_zero` | `rs->south_zero` | **YES** - configurable via `rot_set_conf("south_zero", value)` (rot_conf.c:327). This is the ONLY truly runtime-configurable field in any dump_state output. |
| `rot_type` | `rot->caps->rot_type` | NO - static caps |

#### Amplifier `dump_state` - trivial

Only outputs protocol version (constant `0`) and a hardcoded model name string. No capability data at all.

### What IS truly dynamic state (NOT in `dump_state`)?

These `rig_state` fields change during operation but are **never output by `dump_state`**:
- `rs->current_freq` - actual tuned frequency
- `rs->current_mode` - actual operating mode
- `rs->current_width` - actual passband width
- `rs->current_vfo` - selected VFO
- `rs->tx_vfo` - TX VFO selection
- `rs->transmit` - TX/RX status
- `rs->lo_freq` - LO frequency
- `rs->vfo_comp` - VFO compensation
- `rs->power_now` - current power level

### Conclusion

**`dump_state` is a misnomer.** It dumps *capabilities*, not *state*. Every field it outputs is static or set-once-at-init, with the single exception of rotator `south_zero`/offsets which are configuration parameters.

This means:
1. **A JSON `dump_caps` can fully replace `dump_state`** without any loss of information
2. The JSON output just needs to include the same set of capability fields
3. For rotators, the JSON should read `south_zero` and offsets from `rot_state` (since they're configurable)
4. No need for a separate "state dump" mechanism - all this data is capabilities

### Naming clarification for the codebase

| Current name | What it actually is | Proposed |
|-------------|-------------------|----------|
| `dumpcaps()` function | Human-readable capability dump (reads caps) | Keep, switch to rig_state |
| `dumpstate()` function | Human-readable capability dump (reads rig_state) | DELETE |
| `dump_caps` command ('1') | User-facing capability display | Keep, add JSON mode |
| `dump_state` command (0x8f) | Machine-readable capability dump for network backends | REPLACE with JSON `dump_caps` |

I think the plan is sound.  The backward compatibility is a bit of a sticky issue.  I'm not sure if anyone is doing something like this; some station op has `rigctld` running and has a buddy remote in over the Internet to access it.  In such a case each station would have to upgrade "in-step".  Now, should this be our concern?  Beyond the extent of handling resulting issues, most likely not.  All we can do is explicitly warn of the incompatibility.

That said, as we're treating the 4.7 branch as an LTS of sorts, I think this helps ease the issue to a large extent.  Especially if we can keep radio support in sync between 4.7 and 5.0.0.  Uwe has expressed an intent to follow 5.0 in further development of WSJT-X Improved.

A possible downside is that there may be an assumption that using `rigctld` would act as a bridge between 4.x and 5.x.  To implement this, we need to be clear that 5.0 represents not just C API/ABI changes but also changes to the network daemon protocols.

Some might argue that both protocols should be supported for a major version series, but the implication I get from reading the analysis is that trying to do so would add a lot of duplication and not gain much in reality.

One useful addition could be to make the JSON protocol _always_ respond something to the client, even in case of unknown or invalid commands. The JSON protocol would still be triggered by the `{` character that starts every command, so it would not break existing commands/API.

An unknown command:

```
{"cmd": "unknown_command"}
```

Response to an unknown command: (just giving the code -99 as an example)

```
{"result": -99, "message": "Unknown command"}
```

Invalid JSON:

```
{"this data is not valid JSON}
```

Response for invalid JSON:
```
{"result": -101, "message": "Invalid JSON"}
```

This would make the synchronous command/response nature of the daemon protocol more well-defined.

This discussion may also be related to the possible addition of a JSON protocol for the daemons, see #1999 for introducing a properly machine parseable format for daemon commands and responses.

A more extreme proposal could be that - if JSON protocol will be added soon - Hamlib would only support any new commands with the JSON syntax. This would not break existing commands, again, but would make adapting use of new commands possibly more difficult for existing clients that are not prepared to handle JSON.

EDIT: Maybe disregard this, I'll keep the proposal not related to the JSON protocol - just take this as a FYI that I'm planning to add JSON support for a future-proof protocol format.

Now that I thought of this a bit more, I think we have to preserve NETRIGCTL protocol compatibility between Hamlib 4.x and 5.x for rigs at least (rotators and amplifiers probably don't matter as much, they're seldomly used via the Hamlib NET protocol). I'll just take the case of WSJT-X or a similar app that has got Hamlib client compiled in -> It's not reasonable to require exact version match to provide compatibility between such desktop apps and any rigctld server it connects to.

-> So we can probably remove support for the old "v0" protocol, but the "v1" needs to be preserved both ways: Hamlib 4.x needs to be able to connect to 5.x and vice versa. However, Hamlib 5.x client connecting to a 5.x daemon could already use any new protocol available, so there needs to be some form of detection of Hamlib daemon version.

### Bugs fixed

   - **Bug 1.1** — CTCSS tone table missing 4 tones (171.3, 173.8, 210.7, 218.1 Hz), causing shifted indices for all tones above 167.9 Hz
   -  **Bug 1.2** — RM meter command codes were wrong (e.g., COMP used code 6 instead of 3, SWR used code 7 instead of 6)
   - **Bug 1.3** — FBKIN (full break-in) always failed with `-RIG_EINVAL` because it passed mode=2 to `ftx1_set_breakin()` which only accepts 0/1. Semi vs full break-in is determined by SD delay, not BI mode. Get path also never reported FBKIN active.
   - **Bug 2.1** — VOXDELAY passed raw VD codes (0-33) instead of converting to/from Hamlib tenths-of-seconds
   - **Bug 2.2** — BKINDL passed raw SD codes (0-33) instead of converting to/from Hamlib tenths-of-dots
   - **Bug 2.3** — STRENGTH returned raw 0-255 meter value instead of applying `rig_raw2val()` calibration to dB relative to S9

### Files changed
   - `ftx1_ctcss.c` — corrected tone table
   - `ftx1.h` — updated RM meter command code defines
   - `ftx1.c` — fixed RM meter codes in level map; updated VOXDELAY/BKINDL granularity ranges
   - `ftx1_func.c` — STRENGTH calibration via `rig_raw2val()`; FBKIN/SBKIN dispatcher rewrite
   - `ftx1_audio.c` — VD code↔ms lookup table and VOXDELAY conversion
   - `ftx1_cw.c` — SD code↔ms lookup table, BKINDL conversion, and ms-based delay helpers for break-in

in particular this section:

```
l NR

RPRT -14
```

Actually, NR is defined in Hamlib as a float (0.0–1.0), so the 0.0666667 value is correct — it represents NR level 1 out of 15 steps (1/15 ≈ 0.0667). All Yaesu drivers handle NR this way; it's not something specific to this driver.

To set NR to level 1, you'd use `L NR 0.0666667` (or approximately 0.067). `L NR 1` sets it to the maximum (level 15), though the -14 error you're seeing there is curious — that's RIG_BUSBUSY, which points to a CAT bus issue rather than a parameter problem.

The step size is declared in the driver's level granularity table as 1/15. A client can query it via `L NR ?`, which returns the min, max, and step (e.g. `0.000000..1.000000/0.066667`), and use that to present discrete 0–15 options to the user.

After considering the existing cache workarounds required in ftx1_vfo.c to address Hamlib core cache corruption, I decided to also do a work-around for it in the clarifier code. This should *help* avoid the cache race condition. It's still possible, but clarifier cache follows the same pattern: It also stores state in `newcat_priv_data` and uses it to avoid a read-modify-write race. The key difference is that the VFO cache workaround deals with the Hamlib core's cache being corrupted, while the clarifier cache is purely about tracking radio state to avoid an extra CAT round-trip (which I still think is not worth the squeeze, but it's a design concept promoted in Hamlib so I'll follow along the best I can).

One additional note, the K4 network interface is identical to the serial interface unless you are also trying to do audio processing. In the simple CAT case, you connect to port 9200 with tcp versus opening a serial port. That is for the basic commands. You have Auto-Info mode so you do not need to poll for anything (unlike the Icom network protocol where CI-V Transceive) sends unsolicited packets for frequency and mode changes but not things like RIT, XIT and Split). This is what works in hamlib today so I suspect you are talking about the audio or panadapter. I have the panadapter code in my program on GitHub (TR4QT) but not the audio. Mike AI4QK has his software in GitHub that does implement the audio processing. That program is QK4. 

I tend to believe you are thinking about just CAT control though as there is frankly too much latency in using hamlib to support audio (at least in my experiments). When I compare my native Qt/C++ socket implementation to talk tot he K4 versus hamlib (Over the network as well), I saw higher than expected latency in the connection Typical command round-trip <10ms vs Hamlib 50-100ms. I do not know enough about hamlib to know if that is a function of how it processes messages, replies or both. I left hamlib as an option in TR4QT and TR4W but I recommend the directly-implemented Elecraft, Kenwood and Icom networking implementations, and use hamlib for radios we may not have implemented yet. I mention that as it might be interesting to see if with faster connections such as a network, if the hamlib messaging implementation is revealing some inherent latency that was masked in a serial implementation.

Regarding the design, the following use cases can be supported:

- Application (links to Hamlib) -> Network rig backend (e.g. Icom IC-7610) -> Stream audio or I/Q data over network to/from rig
  - Icom CI-V network protocol is within the scope of the project
- Application (links to Hamlib) -> Network SDR (e.g. some Ettus USRP model) -> Stream I/Q data over network to/from SDR
  - This would require Ettus USRP backend, which is not in the scope of the project
- Application (links to Hamlib) -> Local USB-connected SDR (e.g. RTL-SDR or LimeSDR, or something else over SoapySDR API) -> Stream I/Q data over USB to/from SDR
  - This would require SoapySDR backend, which is not in the scope of the project

The same use cases would be supported remotely over rigctld network connection:

- Application -> Connected to rigctld daemon over network -> Network rig backend (e.g. Icom IC-7610) -> Stream audio or I/Q data over network to/from rig
- Application -> Connected to rigctld daemon over network -> Network SDR (e.g. some Ettus USRP model) -> Stream I/Q data over network to/from SDR
- Application -> Connected to rigctld daemon over network -> Local USB-connected SDR (e.g. RTL-SDR or LimeSDR, or something else over SoapySDR API) -> Stream I/Q data over USB to/from SDR

NOTE: What is not in the scope right now is support of "traditional" audio I/O for streaming audio (e.g. USB sound card provided by a rig), but that could probably be added as "generic" routines for any rig too, e.g. via an OS specific audio API or a library that supports low-latency audio for Linux/Windows/macOS. The API abstraction would allow this anyway.

Additionally, what is not in the scope are "adapters" for applications to record/play back audio for existing applications that only support OS audio devices for communication (e.g. WSJT-X). It's likely something like this could be built as an additional tool supplied with Hamlib, but it still requires virtual audio device handling on at least three OS platforms, which is not trivial :)

The optimal use of the Hamlib data streaming API for digital mode applications would be to use the streamed audio or I/Q data directly within the application, so I'd eventually envision apps like WSJT-X have a built-in support for audio streaming.

With a number of things going on at once, this might be the incorrect place to put these thoughts, but they seem to fit.

@mikaelnousiainen, I know you've expressed a desire to drop the ad hoc `*ctld` protocol in favor of JSON.  How about implementing JSON in separate/new daemons?  `rigctltcp` already exists and while it seems intended for multicast TCP, could it also support unicast TCP without too much trouble?

Would it be possible to have one daemon that could work with multiple devices, say, a radio or two, a rotator or three, and an amplifier or two all at the same time?  The daemon would need to be able to open/close the device port on demand and handle multiple such connections simultaneously, both to backend devices and clients.

It's an ambitious thought.

@N0NB Having a single daemon for handling multiple devices would be more optimal and simpler to use in the end, I agree. But I think it goes to the category of "Hamlib 6.0 plans". Additionally, it would bring little benefit to existing applications, since migrating to a new daemon would require updating both ends and introducing whole new process of controlling the devices.

-> Should we open a "Hamlib 6.0" milestone with this to start the design discussion? It's anyway a fundamental change to how any client would interact with Hamlib.

What I'd propose here is to take a gradual approach: make the JSON parsing/output "pluggable" to the current daemons (or even the CLI apps?). What I mean by pluggable is that there is a separate component with a simple internal API where you can register commands and the parsing/generation of JSON is largely separate from the daemons (unlike the current command/response protocol). EDIT: This way the JSON capabilities could be transferred to a new "combined" daemon with a little less effort.

This will likely mean we need to adapt the existing command handler functions a bit to support output of results in a more structured way - mainly to allow response output in both formats: textual (current) and JSON.

Thoughts? Once I get the first test framework implementation out for review (it's getting there!), I'd very much like to take this task as it would greatly simplify future Hamlib client/application development - and still be backwards compatible fully!

I am Jim, N2ADR, the author of the SDR program Quisk. It connects to WSJT-X using the PC sound system, a constant source of frustration. Ideally, both Quisk and WSJT-X would support Hamlib data streaming and things would be simpler for my users. So my use case is one of the ones you already mentioned:

- Application WSJT-X (internal Hamlib) -> Network rig backend (Quisk) -> Stream audio or I/Q data over network to/from rig; namely received audio from Quisk to WSJT-X and Tx samples from WSJT-X to be transmitted by Quisk.

Note that Quisk takes the place of the Icom IC-7610 radio because it is controlling the real hardware (eg. HL2). I think this is a general feature of all SDR programs, not just Quisk.

I would like to point out that FreeDV digital voice needs four data streams, not just two.

- Quisk received audio -> FreeDV decodes audio -> send decoded audio to Quisk and on to speakers.
- Microphone connected to Quisk -> FreeDV codes audio -> send Tx samples to be transmitted by Quisk.

Although FreeDV could connect to the mic and speakers, Quisk already made that connection and there could be a conflict. Note that FreeDV is acting as a filter or pipeline for both transmit and receive.

Quisk already has builtin Hamlib support and I would be happy to add Hamlib data streaming, especially if WSJT-X and other apps would add it too.

The prompt displayed by the PRC-138 depends on the primary mode the radio
is set to. These main modes correspond to the positions on the Function
switch: SSB, HOP, and ALE.

As explained on page 2-24 of the manual:

*SSB mode is actually single channel mode, not Single Sideband. USB, LSB,
AM, CW, FM can all be accessed when the R/T is in SSB (single channel)
mode.*

Consequently, when the radio is first placed in REMOTE mode, it defaults to
the SSB> prompt.

If you send the ALE command to switch from Single Channel to ALE mode, the
radio will then switch to the ALE> prompt to accept ALE programming
parameters. I hope this clarifies the logic behind the prompts.

Regarding the 'LOW'/'MED'/'HIGH' versus 'low'/'med'/'hi' question: the
radio accepts both lowercase and uppercase for commands and parameters.
However, it consistently responds in uppercase, *except* for the power
settings, where it returns POWER low, POWER med, and POWER hi. This is
likely a firmware bug that was never patched—presumably because military
software developers worldwide had already built their systems around this
specific behavior.

## Verified the three unknowns against a live FTX-1

Ran empirical tests against the same field head + Optima/SPA-1 (fw v1.12). Results:

| Field | BM propagates? | Action |
|-------|---------------|--------|
| freq | ✅ | already in initial commit |
| mode | ✅ | already in initial commit |
| CTCSS (ENC/TSQ + tone) | ✅ | already in initial commit |
| Repeater shift | ✅ | already in initial commit |
| **Clarifier offset** | ✅ | **added** — `CF101<sign><4-digit>;` programs the offset |
| **RIT (RX CLAR flag)** | ✅ | **added** — `CF100<0/1>0000;` toggles RX CLAR |
| **XIT (TX CLAR flag)** | ❌ firmware drops | emit anyway for forward compat, flag in comment |
| **DCS code + mode** | ❌ firmware drops | emit anyway for forward compat, flag in comment |

### Method

For each feature I programmed VFO-B to a known test state, committed with `BM;`, then read the raw 30-char MR response and compared byte positions. DCS and XIT both produced an MR response byte-for-byte identical to the no-tone/no-clarifier baseline, across multiple codes/offsets — conclusive evidence that BM isn't capturing those fields, even though querying VFO-B between the `CT13;`/`CF100.3` set and the `BM;` shows the target state is present.

### Commit

Pushed `c1a2594` on top of the initial `4024cd5`:

- Adds the clarifier `CF` sequence to the rewrite — `rig_set_channel` now persists `chan->rit` correctly
- Documents the two firmware limitations (DCS, XIT) in the function-level comment
- Tightens the cleanup path so VFO-B's clarifier and CT state are explicitly reset on exit, not just FB/MD1

### Verified via rigctl

```
$ rigctl -m 1051 H 1
Frequency: 7050000
mode: LSB
rptr shift: 0
rit: 200
xit: 0
ctcss tone: 0
ctcss sql: 0

# raw MR readback
MR00001007050000+020010110000;
#              ^^^^^^ ^^ — +0200 offset, rx=1, tx=0 ✓
```

Channel 1 round-trips cleanly and both VFOs survive. Full test plan items for freq/mode/clarifier are now checked. DCS and XIT are marked explicitly as firmware limitations rather than untested.
